CDS-bench: Task definitions

84 tasks total: 65 individual task types and 19 composition tasks.

Proposal for evaluating procedural reasoning and constrained design on coding DNA sequences. This document specifies task types, easy and hard prompt templates, scoring rules, and composition tasks.

Draft proposal · Version 0.3 · 26 October 2026

Six examples from the 84 tasks

Four individual tasks and two composition tasks. Each starts from supplied coding DNA and leads to one required answer. For RNA and protein tasks, input preparation is labeled separately. Task titles link to the full definitions.

Biological scope and supplied inputs+

The starting sequence is a complete, spliced CDS with its coding strand and translation start supplied. Tasks do not require gene discovery, splice-site identification, or recognition of a protein family from learned sequence patterns.

What an instance can supply

  • A CDS, or a clearly identified panel of CDSs.
  • A requested edit, motif, guide, pairing map, or coding module.
  • Custom score tables, allowed edits, and numerical bounds.

What the benchmark does not ask for

  • Gene discovery, arbitrary genomic splicing, or isoform prediction.
  • Unannotated biological function, folding, expression, or guide efficacy.
  • Noncoding-RNA maturation or whole-transcript processing.

RNA and protein inputs are obtained by transcribing or translating the supplied CDS. Composition tasks explicitly combine the named operations and specify the final answer.

Shared sequence conventions+

5′→3′ coding DNA; bases may be separated by spaces. All coordinates are 1-based inclusive unless a field explicitly says otherwise. Ordinary translation uses NCBI code 11. First in-frame stop terminates; no stop character appears in the protein.

Synonymous rewrites keep length, first codon, terminal stop, and translated protein fixed. Alternative codes can be separate future rule sets; v0.3 does not silently substitute one.

Easy and hard variants

Easy and hard are paired prompt variants of the same instance. Sequence length, edits, constraints, answer, and validator stay fixed. These labels describe reference support—not separate algorithmic difficulty levels.

variant = easy

Reference supplied

Explain the relevant biology and supply lookup facts: all 64 codons, initiator and stop rules, complementarity, IUPAC expansions, cleavage rules, motif definitions, or residue-property tables.

“Use this codon table and these stop rules…”
variant = hard

Reference knowledge assumed

Ask the shortest unambiguous version using standard biological names. Omit reference explanations. Keep custom instance data and every operational convention needed for a unique, comparable score.

“Translate this CDS with NCBI 11…”

A custom pairing-score table, edit budget, allowed mutation set, or host-specific codon weights must remain supplied in both variants. Those are instance data. Hard prompts should never require guessing an unpublished convention.

A hard prompt can name an established biological reference and expect the model to supply the underlying facts. For example, “use the Kyte–Doolittle scale” requires knowing the hydropathy score for each amino acid. “Translate using NCBI genetic code 11” requires knowing the codon-to-amino-acid assignments, stop codons, and how annotated initiator codons are translated. Easy prompts provide these tables and rules explicitly; hard prompts test whether the model already knows them.

Task schema and scoring

Each task defines its inputs, answer format, and one canonical answer. An instance supplies the actual sequences and conditions. All 84 tasks use the same scorer.

Individual task type
task_type names one of 65 individual operations. For example, cds.translate asks for the protein encoded by a CDS.
Composition task type
composition_type names one of 19 tasks that combine individual operations. For example, pipeline.motif_to_dna translates a CDS, finds a peptide motif, then maps its location back to DNA. Use this field instead of task_type for a composition task.
Variant
variant is easy or hard. It changes biological reference support; both variants share the answer format and correct answer.
Answer format
output_format is scalar for a direct value or simple list, or json for maps and records. output_rules defines every value’s meaning, ordering, precision, and failure form. JSON also has an output_schema for its structure.
Unique reference
objective and selection_rule determine one reference answer, including all tie-breaks. Reference solvers verify constraints, optimality, and any claim of impossibility before evaluation.
Scorer
scorer = exact_match for individual and composition tasks alike. It compares the complete parsed answer with the verified reference.

These are fixed identifiers for question types, not IDs for individual sequences or examples. The lists below enumerate every allowed value and link to its full definition.

Evaluating a response

  1. Read and validate. Extract the answer after the final standalone Final answer: line. Parse its declared format. JSON must satisfy the task’s schema; malformed answers, duplicate keys, and unexpected fields fail validation.
  2. Compare the contents. Apply only the declared formatting normalizations. Compare JSON objects by their keys and values, and lists in their required order. Every requested field must match, including counts and rounded numbers.

Score 1 only when both steps pass; otherwise 0. Report format compliance separately from answer accuracy. Composition tasks receive one score for the complete answer.

For example, the codon-library task expects:

{"status":"ok","codon":"GAK","residue_counts":{"D":1,"E":1}}

Reordering object keys is harmless. Changing a count, omitting a field, or choosing a different codon fails.

Shared answer conventions+

Allow an explanation before the final-answer marker and no trailing prose after the answer. Ignore surrounding whitespace and declared sequence spacing. JSON key order and equivalent numeric spellings such as 1.8500 and 1.85 do not matter. Preserve list order, multiplicities, identifiers, and values. Do not repair malformed JSON or use fuzzy sequence matching.

Round once at the task’s specified precision, with exact halfway cases rounded away from zero; rounded negative zero becomes zero. Use declared reference constants and unrounded intermediate values. CAI optimization on a fixed-length CDS compares exact products of supplied decimal weights before taking roots or rounding.

Empty lists are []. Empty standalone sequences use EMPTY_SEQUENCE; empty sequences inside JSON use "". NONE, INVALID, and IMPOSSIBLE have the meanings defined by their tasks. JSON tasks specify their exact failure objects and use null where required.

TaskDescriptionExpand details
Reverse-complement a CDSdna.reverse_complementGiven a CDS written in one direction, write the complementary DNA strand in its own 5′→3′ direction.

Reverse-complement a CDS

DNA strands pair in opposite directions. The question supplies a CDS as a DNA string and asks for the sequence on the opposite strand. It does not ask where another gene starts or whether the opposite strand encodes a protein.

Replace every base with its DNA partner, then reverse the order so the answer is written 5′→3′. Both steps matter: complementing alone leaves the answer in the wrong direction.

Role in related tasks

A reverse PCR primer must be written in the orientation that binds the opposite strand. CDS-internal primer selection uses this operation to turn the end of the desired amplicon into the reverse-primer sequence.

Method reference: Primer3.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GCT TAA, written 5′→3′.

Procedure. Replace A↔T and C↔G to get TAC CGA ATT in the opposite strand’s 3′→5′ direction. Reverse that entire string to write the answer 5′→3′.

Result. TTA AGC CAT. Complementing and reversing are both necessary.

Final answer:

TTAAGCCAT

Checking the answer. The answer must match the reverse complement base for base; whitespace between bases is ignored.

output_format = scalar

  • Return one uppercase DNA string using A,C,G,T, without spaces, quotes, labels, or a FASTA header.
  • If the resulting sequence has length zero, return the literal token EMPTY_SEQUENCE.

Selection. Apply the stated procedure; the result is uniquely determined by the inputs.

Make the coding RNAdna.transcribeGiven coding-strand DNA, produce its coding RNA by replacing T with U while retaining the order of the bases.

Make the coding RNA

During transcription, RNA polymerase copies the DNA template strand. The resulting RNA matches the opposite, coding strand except that RNA uses uracil (U) where DNA uses thymine (T). Here the supplied DNA is already that coding strand, written 5′→3′, with no introns to remove.

Copy the DNA in the same order and replace every T with U. Keep the start codon and terminal stop codon in the RNA sequence. This creates the RNA input used by editing, pairing, and guide-matching tasks.

Role in related tasks

This is a representation step for following specified RNA edits through to a protein and matching RNA probes against a CDS collection. It supplies the coding RNA on which those operations act; it does not reconstruct a whole transcript.

Example

Inputs. Coding-strand CDS ATG GCT TAA, written 5′→3′.

Procedure. Read left to right, copying A, C, and G unchanged and replacing each T with U. Keep all nine positions, including the stop codon.

Result. Coding RNA AUG GCU UAA.

Final answer:

AUGGCUUAA

Checking the answer. The complete RNA string must be correct and have the same length as the supplied CDS.

Translate DNA to proteincds.translateGiven a CDS and an identified genetic code, return the protein it encodes, ending at the first in-frame stop.

Translate DNA to protein

The CDS is already spliced and oriented correctly. Its first base is the first base of the annotated initiation codon, so the model need not search for an open reading frame. The named genetic code determines how each three-base codon is interpreted.

Read consecutive groups of three bases. Treat the annotated initiator according to NCBI code 11, and end translation at the first stop in that reading frame. Omit the stop and all downstream sequence from the protein answer.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GCT TAA and genetic code 11.

Procedure. Split from base 1 into ATG, GCT, and TAA. The initiator gives M, GCT gives A, and TAA ends translation. Append residues until that first in-frame stop; do not append a stop symbol.

Result. MA. If GGT follows that stop in a supplied segment, the answer is still MA: translation has already ended.

Final answer:

MA

Checking the answer. The final amino-acid string must be exact. A correct prefix followed by extra residues is incorrect.

Role in composition tasks
  • Protein editing and cloning-site cleanup: verifies that the final DNA encodes the requested protein.
  • Tag assembly, cleavage, and mass calculation: supplies the protein sequence used by the downstream cleavage and mass calculations.

Validate a complete CDScds.validateGiven a candidate complete CDS, identify specific problems with its length, initiation codon, or stop codons.

Validate a complete CDS

This is a check of a supplied sequence, not gene prediction. The candidate may have been damaged by an edit. A complete CDS must be long enough to contain an initiator and stop, have a length divisible by three, start with an allowed initiator, and end with a stop.

Check each condition independently and report all violations. Also look for an earlier stop in the established reading frame. The formal labels below name these findings; they are not biological classes to infer from a sequence family.

Related task: Protein-equivalence checking.

Example

Inputs. Candidate CDS GCT TAA GCT TGA.

Procedure. Check each condition separately. The 12-base length is sufficient and divisible by three; the last codon TGA is a stop. But the first codon GCT is not an allowed initiator, and codon 2, TAA, is an earlier in-frame stop.

Result. ["internal_stop", "invalid_start"], sorted by label. Report both failures rather than stopping at the first one.

Final answer:

Map a nucleotide to its codoncoords.nt_to_codonGiven a nucleotide position in a CDS, identify its codon and its position within that codon.

Map a nucleotide to its codon

The question identifies one DNA base by its position in the supplied CDS. Because translation begins at base 1, every base in the translated region belongs to a known group of three.

Count codons from 1. Within the selected codon, use offsets 0, 1, and 2 for its first, second, and third base. Return the codon number, offset, and actual three DNA bases. This provides the bookkeeping needed to connect DNA mutations to protein residues.

Role in related tasks

A DNA-coordinate change needs to be located within a codon before its encoded consequence can be determined. Substitution-effect classification uses that connection to identify the affected residue and compare its original and edited codons.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GCT TAA; nucleotide position 5.

Procedure. Group positions 1–3, 4–6, and 7–9. Position 5 falls in the second group, whose sequence is GCT. Within that group it is the second base, so its zero-based offset is 1.

Result. Codon index 2, offset 1, codon GCT. In general, divide position−1 by 3: the quotient plus 1 gives the codon index, and the remainder gives the offset.

Final answer:

{
  "codon_index": 2,
  "offset": 1,
  "codon": "GCT"
}

Checking the answer. All three returned values must identify the same supplied nucleotide.

Map residues back to DNAcoords.aa_to_ntGiven a range of protein residues, locate the DNA bases encoding that range in the original CDS.

Map residues back to DNA

The question supplies a CDS and an interval of residue positions in its translated protein. It asks where that protein segment is encoded, not where a similar DNA string happens to occur.

Each residue uses three consecutive bases. Include all three bases of the first and last residues in the requested range. Both ends of the returned DNA interval are included. The initiating methionine counts as residue 1.

Role in related tasks

Protein-engineering requests often name residues, while the construct must be changed in DNA. This mapping identifies the codons available for a requested amino-acid substitution or the exact interval removed in a protein deletion construct.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GCT GCT GGT TAA; requested residues 2–3.

Procedure. Translation gives MAAG. Each residue occupies three bases: the first base of residue 2 is 3×2−2 = 4, and the last base of residue 3 is 3×3 = 9.

Result. DNA interval [4,9], containing GCT GCT. Both endpoints are included.

Final answer:

[4,9]

Checking the answer. The nucleotide interval must encode exactly the requested residue interval, with neither missing nor additional codons.

Apply a DNA edit scriptvariant.applyGiven a CDS and a list of DNA replacements, insertions, or deletions, return the edited DNA sequence.

Apply a DNA edit script

The question states exactly which edits to make. Every position refers to the original CDS, so an earlier insertion must not shift the coordinates used to interpret a later edit. No biological effect needs to be predicted in this task.

A replacement names an inclusive interval and its new text; empty replacement text deletes that interval. An insertion names the boundary after an original base. Apply the nonoverlapping changes together and retain every unedited base.

Role in related tasks

Applying an edit script creates the candidate sequence that downstream checks must actually inspect. In DNA edits to peptide readouts, this step precedes translation and digestion, allowing the expected original and mutant peptide products to be compared.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GCT TAA; insert C after original base 3, and replace original base 6 with G.

Procedure. Copy original bases 1–3, insert C, then copy original bases 4–5, replace base 6, and copy bases 7–9. The replacement still addresses the original T at position 6, even though the insertion moves it to position 7 in the output.

Result. ATGCGCGTAA. The task returns the edited DNA; it does not require that the edit preserve a valid CDS.

Final answer:

ATGCGCGTAA

Checking the answer. The entire edited DNA string must be correct. Whether it still encodes a valid protein is checked by other tasks.

Classify a substitution effectvariant.protein_effectGiven an internal DNA substitution, determine whether it preserves the protein, changes residues, or introduces an early stop.

Classify a substitution effect

The supplied change replaces DNA without changing its length and does not touch the initiator or terminal stop. Translate the original and edited CDSs using the same code and reading frame.

An unchanged protein is synonymous. A change to one or more amino acids without an earlier stop is missense. A new earlier stop is stop_gained and takes precedence over other residue changes. Insertions, deletions, and start-codon changes are excluded so these three answers cover every instance.

Practical context

Synonymous, missense, and stop-gained are established sequence-consequence categories used by annotation tools such as Ensembl VEP. This task isolates their codon-comparison logic. The peptide-readout composition follows the sequence changes into expected digest products; neither task infers a variant’s functional impact.

Method reference: Ensembl calculated variant consequences.

Example

Inputs. Reference CDS ATG GGT TAA; replace internal codon 2, GGT, with GAT.

Procedure. Translate the original to MG and the edited CDS to MD. No earlier stop appears, and the complete protein strings differ, so classify the edit as missense. For comparison, replacing GGT with GGC would be synonymous and with TGA would be stop_gained.

Result. missense. The final answer below refers only to the supplied GAT replacement.

Final answer:

missense

Checking the answer. The selected category must follow from the actual translated products, rather than from the number of changed DNA bases.

Determine frame preservationvariant.frame_statusGiven several insertions and deletions, track whether the downstream reading frame is shifted or restored after each edit.

Determine frame preservation

Adding or removing bases changes where subsequent codon boundaries fall. A net length change divisible by three preserves the downstream grouping; a remainder of one or two shifts it. An earlier shift can be undone by a later edit.

Process edit locations in their original order and keep a running total of inserted bases minus deleted bases. After each edit, report that total modulo three: 0 means the original downstream frame, while 1 and 2 indicate the two shifted phases. This does not imply that the intervening protein is unchanged.

Practical context

This check helps review engineered insertions and deletions before interpreting their protein products. Even if a later edit restores the original frame, the intervening translation may have changed. Translation and peptide comparison examines the resulting product beyond this frame-status check.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GCT GGT TAA; insert one base after original position 3, then delete original position 6.

Procedure. Walk through edits in original-coordinate order. Start with net length change 0; insertion makes it +1, and deletion brings it back to 0. After each edit, take that running total modulo 3.

Result. Phases [1,0]. The downstream grouping is shifted between the edits and restored after the deletion; restoring the frame does not restore the intervening residues.

Final answer:

{
  "edits": [
    {
      "edit_index": 1,
      "phase": 1
    },
    {
      "edit_index": 2,
      "phase": 0
    }
  ],
  "final_phase": 0
}

Checking the answer. Every intermediate phase and the final phase must match the cumulative length changes.

  • edits contains one record per supplied edit, in original-coordinate processing order. edit_index is the edit’s 1-based index in the supplied edit list, not its position in the sorted list. phase is cumulative (inserted bases minus deleted bases) modulo 3 immediately after that edit.
  • Sort edits by their first affected original base; an insertion after base k uses k+1. Break equal-coordinate ties by original edit_index. final_phase is the last phase, or 0 when there are no edits.

Compare encoded proteinscds.protein_equivalenceGiven two CDSs, determine whether their complete translated protein sequences are identical.

Compare encoded proteins

Two different DNA sequences can encode the same protein because several codons can specify the same amino acid. DNA string equality therefore cannot answer this question.

Translate both CDSs under NCBI code 11, including its initiator treatment and first-stop termination. Compare the resulting amino-acid strings, including their lengths. Return a yes/no answer; no judgement about expression or function is required.

Practical context

This is a correctness check for synonymous engineering: DNA changes are acceptable only if the encoded protein stays the same. Cloning-site removal with GC control needs this check so that manufacturing or assembly constraints do not silently alter the intended protein.

Method reference: DNA Chisel examples.

Example

Inputs. CDSs ATG GGT TAA and ATG GGC TAA.

Procedure. Translate each separately: both start with M, GGT and GGC both give G, and TAA terminates. Compare the resulting amino-acid strings, not the DNA strings.

Result. true: both encode exactly MG.

Final answer:

true

Checking the answer. Both translated products must be identical for the answer to be true.

Resolve an ambiguous codonambiguity.codon_setGiven an internal codon containing uncertain-base symbols, list every amino acid or stop it could encode.

Resolve an ambiguous codon

An IUPAC symbol can stand for several possible DNA bases. For example, N means any of A, C, G, or T. The question identifies one ambiguous codon inside an otherwise defined CDS; its possible meanings are determined by expanding those symbols.

Form every concrete codon allowed by the symbols, translate each using internal codon meanings, and collect the distinct results. Report each amino acid once, even if several codons produce it. Include STOP if any expansion is a stop.

Role in related tasks

An ambiguous triplet can represent uncertain base calls or a deliberately degenerate synthesis instruction. Degenerate-library enumeration uses the same expansion to establish exactly which amino acids and stops an oligonucleotide mixture could encode.

Method reference: SwiftLib.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG TAN TAA; inspect internal codon 2. N allows A, C, G, or T.

Procedure. Expand TAN into TAA, TAC, TAG, and TAT. Translate each internally: STOP, Y, STOP, and Y. Remove repeated outcomes.

Result. The distinct possibilities are {STOP, Y}. Two stop codons still contribute only one STOP member to this set.

Final answer:

["STOP","Y"]

Checking the answer. The answer must contain every possible result and no result excluded by the ambiguity symbols.

Answer format and selection · scalar+

output_format = scalar

  • Return one bracketed list. Use JSON list syntax with double-quoted strings where applicable, but no enclosing object. Return [] when there are no entries.
  • List each possible internal amino acid once as its uppercase one-letter symbol; use the string STOP for a stop codon. Sort strings in ASCII order, including STOP.

Selection. Apply the stated procedure; the result is uniquely determined by the inputs.

  • codon_index 1-based internal codon index

Assess an ambiguous stopambiguity.stop_certaintyGiven an ambiguous internal codon, decide whether a stop is impossible, possible, or unavoidable.

Assess an ambiguous stop

The uncertain bases describe a set of possible concrete codons, not a probability distribution. The task asks what can be concluded about stopping from that set alone.

Expand the selected codon. If none of its expansions is a stop, return never. If every expansion is a stop, return guaranteed. If both stop and non-stop expansions exist, return possible. This evaluates certainty without guessing which bases were actually present.

Role in related tasks

A mixed codon may produce a stop in only some synthesized molecules. This distinction matters in designing and auditing a mutagenesis library, where an apparently useful ambiguity code can also create unwanted truncated products.

Method reference: SwiftLib.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG TAN TAA; inspect internal codon 2. N allows A, C, G, or T.

Procedure. Expand TAN into TAA, TAC, TAG, and TAT. Two of the four codons are stops, so a stop is possible but not guaranteed. By comparison, TAR is guaranteed and GCN is never a stop.

Result. possible. This is a logical classification, not an estimated probability.

Final answer:

possible

Checking the answer. The category must account for all allowed expansions, not just one representative codon.

  • Return exactly one lowercase token: never, possible, or guaranteed.

Count sense codonsstats.codon_countsGiven a CDS, count how often each DNA codon occurs in its translated region.

Count sense codons

The CDS establishes the groups of three to count. This is different from counting every three-base substring: overlapping substrings between codon boundaries do not contribute.

Count the initiator and all subsequent sense codons, but omit the terminal stop. Report the original DNA spellings, so synonymous codons such as GGT and GGC have separate counts even though both encode glycine.

Role in related tasks

Codon counts are the raw observations behind codon-usage comparisons and reference tables. Counts from a chosen reference gene set can support the preference weights used in CAI, while counts from a candidate CDS describe how its synonymous choices differ from that reference.

Method reference: Codon Statistics Database.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GGT GGT GGC TAA.

Procedure. Read aligned triplets from base 1. Exclude terminal TAA and add one to the count of each remaining DNA triplet as it is encountered. Keep GGT and GGC separate even though both encode G.

Result. {ATG:1, GGT:2, GGC:1}. Count codons, not every overlapping three-base substring.

Final answer:

{
  "ATG": 1,
  "GGC": 1,
  "GGT": 2
}

Checking the answer. Each observed codon’s count must be exact; the counts must sum to the number of sense codons.

output_format = json

  • Return JSON only after the final-answer marker: exactly the named fields, correct JSON types, and no additional fields or duplicate object keys. Object-key order and insignificant JSON whitespace do not matter.
  • The answer object itself maps each observed aligned DNA sense codon to its positive integer occurrence count. Include the initiator, exclude the terminal stop, and omit absent codons. Keys are uppercase three-base codons; values count codon occurrences, not amino acids or overlapping triplets.

Selection. Apply the stated procedure; the result is uniquely determined by the inputs.

Calculate total GCstats.gc_fractionGiven a CDS, calculate the fraction of all its DNA bases that are G or C.

Calculate total GC

GC content is a sequence-composition measurement. It counts bases across the complete supplied CDS, including its initiation and terminal stop codons.

Add the number of G and C bases and divide by total sequence length. Return a fraction between 0 and 1, rounded as requested. This task does not ask whether that composition is biologically preferable.

Practical context

Overall GC is a quick composition check during synthetic-gene design. Manufacturing constraints often concern local extremes as well, so windowed GC checks and synonymous GC repair turn this simple measurement into a more useful construct-design check.

Method reference: Twist gene-design resources.

Example

Inputs. Complete CDS ATG GCT TAA.

Procedure. Count G and C across all nine bases: ATG contributes 1, GCT contributes 2, and TAA contributes 0. Divide their total, 3, by the sequence length, 9.

Result. 3/9 = 0.333333 after rounding to six decimal places.

Final answer:

0.333333

Checking the answer. The number is checked against the calculated fraction at the stated precision.

Answer format and selection · scalar+

Calculate third-position GCstats.gc3_fractionGiven a CDS, calculate GC content using only the third base of each sense codon.

Calculate third-position GC

Third codon positions are useful to examine separately because many synonymous choices differ there. The question asks for GC3, not the overall fraction of G and C in the CDS.

Take the third base of every sense codon, including the initiator and excluding the terminal stop. Divide the number of those selected bases that are G or C by the number of selected bases. Other codon positions do not enter the calculation.

Practical context

GC3 is used in comparative codon-usage analysis to describe compositional bias at third codon positions, where many synonymous alternatives occur. Comparing it with other codon-bias statistics helps separate a sequence’s overall compositional tendency from more specific codon preferences.

Method reference: Codon Statistics Database.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GCT TAA.

Procedure. Exclude the terminal stop, then take only the third base of each remaining codon: G from ATG and T from GCT. One of those two selected bases is G or C.

Result. GC3 = 1/2 = 0.5. The denominator is two sense codons, not nine DNA bases.

Final answer:

0.500000

Checking the answer. The answer must use the specified codon positions and denominator, with the requested rounding.

Locate GC-window violationsstats.gc_windowsGiven a window length and an allowed GC range, identify local parts of a CDS whose composition falls outside that range.

Locate GC-window violations

A whole-CDS average can hide a short GC-rich or GC-poor region. The question therefore gives a window length: the number of consecutive DNA bases to examine at a time. It also gives the lowest and highest acceptable GC fractions.

Slide that window one base at a time across the CDS and calculate GC content separately for every full window. Return the starting positions of windows below the minimum or above the maximum. Values exactly on either bound are acceptable.

Practical context

A CDS can have acceptable overall GC but contain a locally extreme region that complicates synthesis or amplification. This measurement locates such regions; synonymous window repair changes them, and the cloning-and-GC composition combines that repair with assembly-site constraints.

Method reference: Twist gene-design resources.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GGG TAA; window length 6; allowed GC fraction from 1/3 through 1/2, inclusive.

Procedure. Slide a six-base window by one base. The four windows contain 4, 4, 4, and 3 G/C bases. The bounds permit 2 or 3 G/C bases per window, so the first three fail and the fourth passes.

Result. Violating window starts [1,2,3]. Report every failing start, including overlapping windows.

Final answer:

[1,2,3]

Checking the answer. The returned positions must identify all failing windows, including overlapping ones.

Calculate codon adaptation indexstats.caiGiven a CDS and codon-preference weights, calculate a codon adaptation index from those weights.

Calculate codon adaptation index

The question supplies a numerical preference weight for each relevant codon. These weights define the reference against which the CDS is compared; the model is not expected to infer them from an organism name.

Hosts differ in the availability of tRNAs that decode synonymous codons, which can affect translation efficiency. Highly expressed host genes provide an empirical reference for codon preferences. CAI measures resemblance to that reference, giving one guide for designing a gene for expression in that host. Broader methods such as LinearDesign combine CAI with RNA folding models to optimize codon usage and structural stability together.

Look up the weight of each sense codon after the initiator and take their geometric mean. The initiator and terminal stop are excluded. The geometric mean combines preference across the sequence while retaining sensitivity to poorly weighted codons.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GGT GCT TAA; supplied weights GGT = 1.0 and GCT = 0.25.

Procedure. Exclude the initiator ATG and stop TAA. Multiply the remaining weights: 1.0×0.25 = 0.25. Because there are two included codons, take the square root of that product. For n codons, the same rule takes the nth root.

Result. CAI = √0.25 = 0.5, reported as 0.500000 at six decimal places.

Final answer:

0.500000

Checking the answer. The calculated value must use the supplied weights and specified codon exclusions.

This calculation is a prerequisite for synonymous codon-preference optimization, and is used in optimization with RNA constraints.

Find nucleotide patternsdna.motif_positionsGiven a DNA pattern, locate every matching interval in the CDS on the requested strand or strands.

Find nucleotide patterns

Restriction enzymes recognize particular DNA sequences: for example, EcoRI recognizes GAATTC. That is one concrete reason to locate a short pattern in a CDS. The pattern is supplied here and may include IUPAC symbols allowing several bases at a position.

Check every possible starting position, including starts that cross codon boundaries and overlap other matches. If both strands are requested, also search for the reverse-complement pattern. Report all intervals on the coordinate axis of the original CDS, with the matching strand.

Role in related tasks

Locating restriction-enzyme recognition sites is a routine prerequisite for cloning-site cleanup. Motif removal uses these hits to eliminate unwanted sites, including sites crossing codon boundaries, while preserving the protein.

Method reference: GoldenMutagenesis domestication.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GGT TAA; DNA pattern GG; search the forward strand.

Procedure. Try the pattern at each possible start, advancing by one base even after a match. It matches bases 3–4 and 4–5. The first match crosses a codon boundary, and the two matches overlap.

Result. [(3,4,+), (4,5,+)]. Neither overlap nor codon boundaries suppress a hit.

Final answer:

[
  {
    "start": 3,
    "end": 4,
    "strand": "+"
  },
  {
    "start": 4,
    "end": 5,
    "strand": "+"
  }
]

Checking the answer. Every matching interval and strand must be present. Identical hits from a palindromic pattern are reported only once.

REFERENCE
IUPAC DNA ambiguity: A=A; C=C; G=G; T=T; R=AG; Y=CT; S=CG; W=AT; K=GT; M=AC; B=CGT; D=AGT; H=ACT; V=ACG; N=ACGT. An ambiguous symbol represents a set, not a fifth nucleotide. Different positions expand independently.

A coding DNA strand is written 5′→3′. Its coding RNA has the same order of bases with U in place of T. The opposite strand is antiparallel. DNA complement: A↔T, C↔G. A reverse complement complements every base and reverses the sequence.

Find a supplied peptide patternprotein.motif_positionsTranslate the CDS and find every protein segment matching a supplied amino-acid pattern.

Find a supplied peptide pattern

A supplied peptide pattern can describe a real enzyme-recognition site. For example, TEV protease cleavage uses ENLYFQG in this benchmark. More general patterns can name an exact residue, allow any residue, list alternatives, or exclude selected residues.

Match the pattern at every protein position and return the residue intervals of complete matches. Include overlaps. This identifies a sequence pattern only; it does not require recognizing a protein family or deciding whether a matched site is functional.

Role in related tasks

An explicitly supplied peptide pattern can mark a protease site or an engineered sequence feature. Motif-to-DNA mapping locates its encoding codons for a later edit, and motif removal changes a permitted occurrence. The task does not infer a motif’s function from its sequence.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG AAT GCT TCT AAT CCT TCT AAT GGT ACT TAA; pattern N{P}[ST].

Procedure. Translate to MNASNPSNGT, then test every three-residue window for N, a non-P residue, and S or T. NAS at residues 2–4 and NGT at 8–10 pass; NPS at 5–7 fails its middle-position test.

Result. Protein intervals [(2,4), (8,10)].

Final answer:

[[2,4],[8,10]]

Checking the answer. The result must include exactly the matching residue intervals, numbered from the protein’s first residue.

  • Coordinates refer to the translated protein. Include all overlapping matches once each.

Locate N-glycosylation sequonsprotein.nglyco_sequonsTranslate the CDS and identify protein positions matching the conventional N-glycosylation sequon pattern.

Locate N-glycosylation sequons

N-linked glycosylation attaches a sugar chain to an asparagine side chain in a protein. Its common acceptor pattern is asparagine, then any residue except proline, then serine or threonine: N–X–S/T with X≠P. A matching three-residue sequence is called a sequon.

Find every occurrence of that three-residue pattern and report the position of its first residue. Do not decide whether the protein reaches a cellular compartment where glycosylation occurs or whether a particular site is actually modified.

Practical context

Sequon scanning identifies candidate sites to inspect when designing or reviewing a protein for N-glycosylation studies. It is a sequence screen: actual modification depends on the expression system and protein context. Residue-to-DNA mapping can locate the codons if a candidate site is selected for mutagenesis.

Method reference: PROSITE N-glycosylation pattern.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG AAT GCT TCT AAT CCT TCT AAT GGT ACT TAA.

Procedure. Translate to MNASNPSNGT. For each N, inspect the next two residues: NAS passes N–non-P–S/T, NPS fails because of P, and NGT passes. Record the starting N of each passing window.

Result. Sequon starts [2,8]. This reports pattern positions, not experimentally occupied glycosylation sites.

Final answer:

[2,8]

Checking the answer. All matching start positions must be correct, including overlapping matches.

Count amino acidsprotein.residue_countsTranslate a CDS and count the number of each amino acid in its protein product.

Count amino acids

This measures protein composition rather than DNA composition or codon usage. Different synonymous codons contribute to the same amino-acid count after translation.

Translate the CDS, then count each residue in the resulting protein. Include the initiating methionine and do not count the stop. Return counts for residues that occur; the order of residues in the protein is not part of this answer.

Role in related tasks

Composition counts supply inputs to mass, charge, and isoelectric-point calculations. The protein-measurements composition connects a CDS to these descriptors, which can support product identification and purification planning.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GCT GCT GGT TAA.

Procedure. Translate to MAAG. Start an empty count map and increment one entry per residue: M, then A twice, then G. Do not count the terminal DNA stop as a residue.

Result. {M:1, A:2, G:1}.

Final answer:

{
  "A": 2,
  "G": 1,
  "M": 1
}

Checking the answer. The residue counts must be exact and sum to the translated protein’s length.

Calculate peptide massprotein.monoisotopic_massTranslate a CDS and calculate the neutral monoisotopic mass of its unmodified protein product.

Calculate peptide mass

Mass calculations depend on a chemical convention. This task specifies an unmodified linear protein with free ends, without removing the initiator or forming disulfide bonds. Monoisotopic mass uses the masses of the specified isotopes rather than an average over isotopes.

A chain of n amino acids has n−1 peptide bonds; its chemical composition differs from n free amino acids by n−1 water molecules. The tabulated residue masses already subtract one water per residue. Sum those residue masses and add one water to recover the complete chain with free ends. Each separate digestion product gets its own water contribution.

Practical context

Theoretical peptide masses help interpret mass-spectrometry measurements when checking a protein’s identity or processing. Tag assembly, cleavage, and mass calculation applies this to the actual cleavage products, where a retained tag or cleavage scar changes the expected mass.

Method reference: ExPASy PeptideMass documentation.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GCT TAA, encoding MA; residue masses M = 131.040485 Da and A = 71.037114 Da; water = 18.010565 Da.

Procedure. Look up and add each incorporated residue mass once, then add one water molecule for the complete linear product: 131.040485 + 71.037114 + 18.010565.

Result. 220.088164 Da. Water is added once per resulting molecule, not once per residue.

Final answer:

220.0882

Checking the answer. The declared residue-mass sum plus one water must round to the reported four-decimal mass.

Calculate mean hydropathyprotein.mean_hydropathyTranslate a CDS and average the encoded residues’ scores on the Kyte–Doolittle hydropathy scale.

Calculate mean hydropathy

Amino-acid side chains differ in how favorably they interact with water. The Kyte–Doolittle hydropathy scale assigns experimentally informed scores to that tendency: positive values are more hydrophobic, while negative values are more hydrophilic. These are a published scale, not arbitrary scores invented for this task.

Look up the score for each residue and calculate the ordinary arithmetic mean across the whole protein. This is a summary measurement; it is not a request to classify the protein as a transporter or predict its location.

Practical context

Mean hydropathy is a standard descriptive property reported by tools such as ProtParam. It summarizes overall residue composition; hydropathy analyses that seek local hydrophobic segments use positional windows instead. Here it belongs in a protein-characterization report, rather than serving as a standalone membrane-localization prediction.

Method reference: ExPASy ProtParam documentation.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GCT TAA, encoding MA; Kyte–Doolittle scores M = 1.9 and A = 1.8.

Procedure. Look up one score per residue, add them, and divide by the number of residues: (1.9 + 1.8)/2. Repeated residues would contribute repeatedly.

Result. Mean hydropathy 1.85.

Final answer:

1.8500

Checking the answer. The answer must use the named scale and average all translated residues with equal weight.

Digest with trypsin rulesprotein.trypsin_digestTranslate the CDS and list the peptide fragments produced by a specified complete trypsin-cleavage model.

Digest with trypsin rules

Trypsin is a real protein-digesting enzyme used to generate peptides for mass spectrometry. Its specificity favors cutting after lysine (K) or arginine (R). The benchmark uses the familiar simplified rule: cut after K/R unless the following residue is proline (P). Actual cleavage efficiencies and exceptions are not calculated.

Apply the rule at every eligible bond, allowing no missed cuts, and retain fragments at both ends. Return fragments in their original order, together with their inclusive residue intervals in the original protein.

Practical context

In-silico digestion predicts peptide sequences to compare with proteomics measurements. Diagnostic-peptide selection looks for products that distinguish related proteins, while variant-to-peptide comparison shows how a sequence change alters the expected digest.

Method reference: ExPASy PeptideMass documentation.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GCT AAA CGT CCT GCT AAA TAA, encoding MAKRPAK.

Procedure. Scan each protein bond. Cut after K at position 3; do not cut after R at position 4 because P follows it. The final K ends the last fragment and does not create an empty fragment.

Result. [(1,3,MAK), (4,7,RPAK)], in protein order.

Final answer:

[
  {
    "start": 1,
    "end": 3,
    "peptide": "MAK"
  },
  {
    "start": 4,
    "end": 7,
    "peptide": "RPAK"
  }
]

Checking the answer. Both peptide sequences and their original residue intervals must be correct.

  • Each record represents one nonempty tryptic fragment. start and end are 1-based inclusive residue positions in the complete translated protein; peptide is its exact uppercase sequence. Return fragments in N-to-C order (increasing start), retaining identical sequences from different intervals. Do not include empty terminal fragments. An empty protein gives [].

Select a distinguishing peptideprotein.diagnostic_peptideFrom a target CDS and comparison CDSs, choose a digest peptide that occurs only in the target’s protein.

Select a distinguishing peptide

You are given a target CDS encoding the protein you want to identify, and comparison CDSs encoding other proteins you want to distinguish it from. The comparison set is called the background in the input fields. Translate and digest each sequence using the same trypsin rule. An identifying peptide must occur in the target digest and in none of the comparison digests.

Keep target peptides whose lengths lie within the supplied minimum and maximum. Select the shortest eligible peptide, using alphabetical order to break a tie. Return NONE if none qualifies. Uniqueness applies only to the supplied comparison set, not an entire proteome.

Practical context

A peptide unique to one candidate protein is a starting point for choosing an identifying mass-spectrometry readout. The CDS-panel composition derives such candidates from actual digests. Subsequent assay design must also consider whether the peptide can be detected reliably, not just whether its sequence is unique.

Method reference: ExPASy PeptideMass documentation.

Example

Inputs. Target CDS ATG GCT AAA GCT GGT AAA TAA; one comparison CDS ATG GCT AAA GGT GCT AAA TAA. Peptides must be exactly 3 amino acids long.

Procedure. The CDSs differ at codons 4–5: the target has GCT GGT (Ala–Gly), while the comparison has GGT GCT (Gly–Ala). Translate to target MAKAGK and comparison MAKGAK. Trypsin digestion gives target MAK | AGK and comparison MAK | GAK. Discard MAK because both proteins produce it. The remaining target peptide, AGK, meets the length requirement.

Result. AGK. It distinguishes the target from this comparison protein because only the target digest contains it. If the comparison CDS were identical to the target, no peptide would qualify and the answer would be NONE.

Final answer:

AGK

Checking the answer. The selected peptide must satisfy panel uniqueness and length limits, and obey the stated selection order. Detectability in a mass spectrometer is not scored.

Answer format and selection · scalar+

output_format = scalar

  • Return the complete uppercase one-letter amino-acid string without spaces, quotes, a FASTA header, or a terminal stop symbol.
  • Return NONE if no target-only peptide meets the length limits.

Selection. From eligible target-only peptide sequences, choose the shortest, then the ASCII-lexicographically smallest sequence. Multiple copies of one sequence do not create separate choices.

When there is no result or no feasible design:

NONE

Calculate model charge at a pHprotein.charge_at_phTranslate a CDS and estimate its protein’s net charge at a specified pH using supplied ionization parameters.

Calculate model charge at a pH

Some amino-acid side chains and the two ends of a protein gain or lose protons as pH changes. The question supplies a pH and pKa values, which determine the fractions of sites treated as charged in the declared calculation.

Count each relevant acidic or basic side chain and both free termini, calculate its contribution with the Henderson–Hasselbalch relation, and add the contributions. The model treats sites independently; it does not account for a folded protein changing a site’s environment.

Practical context

Estimated protein charge helps choose a pH and resin type for ion-exchange purification, which separates molecules through charge-dependent binding. This calculation supplies a first estimate from the sequence; purification methods then test suitable buffers and binding conditions.

Method reference: Cytiva ion-exchanger selection guide.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GCT TAA, encoding MA; pH = 6; supplied pKa values N terminus = 8 and C terminus = 4.

Procedure. MA has no ionizable side chains in this model. Its N terminus contributes +1/(1+10^(6−8)) ≈ +0.990099. Its C terminus contributes −1/(1+10^(4−6)) ≈ −0.990099. Add all site contributions.

Result. Net model charge 0.000000. Other proteins also require contributions from every applicable side chain.

Final answer:

0.0000

Checking the answer. The net charge must match the supplied-pKa model at the requested pH and precision.

Answer format and selection · scalar+

output_format = scalar

  • Return only the net charge as a decimal number with exactly 4 digits after the decimal point. Do not add a unit, percent sign, equation, or field name.
  • Round once at the end to nearest, with exact halfway cases rounded away from zero. Use 0 rather than -0 after rounding. Use the declared reference constants and unrounded intermediate values.

Selection. Apply the stated procedure; the result is uniquely determined by the inputs.

Calculate the isoelectric point (pI)protein.isoelectric_pointTranslate a CDS, then find the pH where the protein’s calculated positive and negative charges cancel.

Calculate the isoelectric point (pI)

The isoelectric point (pI) is the pH at which a protein’s positive and negative charges balance, giving a total charge of zero. The inputs are a CDS and pKa values for the groups that can carry charge. A group’s pKa is the pH at which its calculated contribution is half of its fully charged value.

The charge calculation is a fixed arithmetic approximation: treat each group separately and add its contribution. Count one N terminus, one C terminus, and each occurrence of the listed amino-acid side chains. Use the supplied pKa for each group in the formulas below; all other side chains contribute zero.

Increasing pH decreases this calculated total charge. Each instance is chosen so positive and negative contributions cancel once between pH 0 and pH 14. Those two pH numbers are the initial search bounds.

  • Positive groups: N terminus and K, R, H side chains: +1 / (1 + 10^(pH − pKa)).
  • Negative groups: C terminus and D, E, C, Y side chains: −1 / (1 + 10^(pKa − pH)).

Simple algorithm: repeatedly halve the pH range

  1. Translate the CDS and count the charge-carrying groups in that protein, including both free ends.
  2. Start with a lower pH of 0 and an upper pH of 14. Calculate total charge at their midpoint, initially pH 7.
  3. If the total is positive, the zero-charge pH is higher: replace the lower pH with the midpoint. If negative, it is lower: replace the upper pH. If the total is exactly zero, that pH is the answer.
  4. Repeat the midpoint calculation on the remaining pH range until its width is less than 0.001. Report that range’s midpoint rounded to two decimal places.

Practical context

A protein’s pI helps select conditions for ion-exchange purification and isoelectric focusing. Together with charge at a chosen pH, it indicates which side of the charge transition an operating condition lies on, before testing the behavior experimentally.

Method reference: Cytiva ion-exchanger selection guide.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GCT TAA, encoding MA; N-terminal pKa = 8 and C-terminal pKa = 4. MA has no charge-carrying side chains in this calculation. Start the search from pH 0 to pH 14.

Procedure. At the first midpoint, pH 7, total charge is about −0.0899, so search pH 0–7. The next midpoint, pH 3.5, gives about +0.7597, so search pH 3.5–7. Keep replacing one endpoint this way; after 14 midpoint checks, the range is approximately pH 5.99939–6.00024.

Result. pI = 6.00. As a check, at pH 6 the terminal contributions are approximately +0.990099 and −0.990099, summing to zero.

Final answer:

6.00

Checking the answer. Find the unique zero-charge pH under the supplied pKa values and formulas, then round it to two decimal places. That rounded value is the reference answer.

Coding RNA analysis

Editing, pairing, cleavage, and sequence targeting.

9 tasks
rna task definitions
TaskDescriptionExpand details
Apply specified RNA editsrna.apply_editsTranscribe a CDS, apply explicitly listed changes to its coding RNA, and return the edited RNA sequence.

Apply specified RNA edits

RNA editing changes RNA after transcription. One real example is APOBEC1-mediated C-to-U editing of apolipoprotein B mRNA: a CAA codon becomes the UAA stop codon, producing a shorter protein. Here the editing positions and replacement bases are supplied, rather than predicted from an enzyme’s recognition preferences.

Apply all changes using positions in that original RNA, keeping RNA’s U alphabet. Replacement text may also insert or delete bases. Later edit coordinates are not shifted by earlier changes. Translation of the edited product is a separate component.

Role in related tasks

When RNA-editing events have been measured or explicitly proposed, their consequences must be evaluated on the edited sequence. Edit-to-protein analysis uses this step to establish the transcript that is translated; edit-to-fragment analysis instead derives a possible RNA sequence-QC readout.

Example

Inputs. CDS-derived RNA AUG GCU UAA; replace original RNA position 6 with C.

Procedure. Locate position 6 in the original RNA: it is U, the third base of GCU. Replace only that position and copy all other bases. For multiple edits, keep using original coordinates.

Result. AUG GCC UAA.

Final answer:

AUGGCCUAA

Checking the answer. The complete edited RNA must match the specified changes and preserve every unedited base.

Answer format and selection · scalar+

Translate coding RNArna.translateTranslate coding RNA derived from a CDS, including RNA that has undergone supplied edits.

Translate coding RNA

This component accepts RNA rather than DNA so an edited transcript can be passed directly into translation. In an isolated prompt, the RNA is transcribed from the supplied CDS; in a composition, it can be the output of the RNA-editing task.

Read RNA codons from the established first base using the named genetic code, with U in place of DNA’s T. Stop at the first in-frame stop and omit that stop from the answer. Do not silently switch back to translating the original DNA.

Role in related tasks

The useful distinction from direct DNA translation appears in the RNA-editing composition: the protein must be derived from the edited coding RNA, which can differ from the product predicted from the original DNA. This task supplies that downstream translation step.

Example

Inputs. Coding RNA AUG GGU UAA, obtained after a supplied edit to CDS-derived RNA.

Procedure. Read triplets from the original translation start. AUG contributes M, GGU contributes G, and UAA terminates. Use the edited RNA’s codons rather than reverting to the original DNA.

Result. MG.

Final answer:

MG

Checking the answer. The returned protein must come from the actual RNA input, including its edits and stopping point.

Check specified RNA pairsrna.pair_compatibilityGiven a CDS-derived RNA and specified paired positions, identify pairs whose bases cannot form an allowed pair.

Check specified RNA pairs

Complementary stretches of one RNA can bind each other, forming paired stems and unpaired loops. A–U and C–G are the canonical base-pair types. The supplied position pairs state which contacts to check; the task does not discover the fold.

Read the two bases at each listed pair and test their compatibility. Real RNA can also form G–U wobble pairs, but this benchmark deliberately permits only A–U and C–G in either direction. Return the incompatible position pairs only.

Role in related tasks

This is a local consistency check after changing bases in a proposed RNA stem. Pair repair with protein verification uses it to test whether a synonymous redesign restores the requested contacts. The structure is supplied, so the check does not establish that those contacts form experimentally.

Example

Inputs. Coding RNA AUG GCU UAA; supplied pairs (1,7), (3,5), and (2,6).

Procedure. Look up the two bases at each pair: A–U, G–C, and U–U. Compare each with the allowed set AU, UA, GC, and CG. Collect pairs that fail instead of searching for a new fold.

Result. Incompatible pairs [(2,6)].

Final answer:

[[2,6]]

Checking the answer. The answer must identify every incompatible supplied pair. It does not assert that the RNA actually adopts the supplied structure.

Decode a pairing maprna.dotbracket_to_pairsConvert a supplied dot-bracket annotation for coding RNA into explicit pairs of nucleotide positions.

Decode a pairing map

Dot-bracket notation describes an RNA pairing map. A dot marks an unpaired base; matching opening and closing parentheses identify a pair. The annotation has the same length as the RNA.

Match the parentheses and report their 1-based positions. Nested pairs are allowed, but this task excludes crossing pairs called pseudoknots. This is notation interpretation rather than prediction of a structure from the sequence.

Role in related tasks

Dot-bracket notation is a common output of RNA structure software. Converting it to coordinate pairs makes the annotation usable in explicit sequence checks, such as pair compatibility and the simplified structure-dependent cleavage model.

Method reference: ViennaRNA.

Example

Inputs. Coding RNA AUG GCU UAA; annotation (.(.).).., one character per base.

Procedure. Scan left to right, storing opening-parenthesis positions. Push 1, then 3; the close at 5 pairs with the most recently stored opening, 3. The close at 7 then pairs with 1. Ignore dots and sort the pairs.

Result. [(1,7), (3,5)]. This is parenthesis matching, not structure prediction.

Final answer:

[[1,7],[3,5]]

Checking the answer. Every parenthesis pair must become exactly one correct coordinate pair.

Digest coding RNA with RNase T1 rulesrna.t1_digestTranscribe a CDS and split its RNA into fragments using an RNase T1 rule, optionally restricted by a supplied pairing map.

Digest coding RNA with RNase T1 rules

RNase T1 is a real guanosine-specific RNA-cutting enzyme originally obtained from the fungus Aspergillus oryzae. It cleaves the RNA backbone immediately after G, on the G’s 3′ side. The G therefore remains at the end of the upstream fragment. Choosing G reflects this enzyme’s biochemical specificity.

RNase T1 acts preferentially on single-stranded RNA. The question either treats every G as eligible or uses a supplied pairing map to allow cuts only at unpaired G bases. Complete cleavage and that fixed accessibility mask are benchmark simplifications.

Scan for eligible cuts, split the sequence, and return the fragments in sequence order with their original RNA coordinates. When a pairing map is supplied, keep it fixed rather than refolding after each cut.

Practical context

RNase fragment mapping is used in RNA sequence characterization, including mRNA quality control. This task supplies the simple sequence-to-fragments step. Practical mapping combines digestion with mass spectrometry and may use complementary or partial digests to resolve fragments that a single complete digest cannot distinguish.

Method reference: RNA and mRNA sequence mapping by mass spectrometry.

Example

Inputs. Coding RNA AUG GCU UAA; accessibility = all, with an empty pair map.

Procedure. The enzyme-specific rule identifies G at positions 3 and 4. Cut immediately after each: AUG|G|CUUAA. Each G stays on the left side of its cut; preserve every base exactly once.

Result. [(1,3,AUG), (4,4,G), (5,9,CUUAA)]. Consecutive G bases produce a one-base middle fragment.

Final answer:

[
  {
    "start": 1,
    "end": 3,
    "fragment": "AUG"
  },
  {
    "start": 4,
    "end": 4,
    "fragment": "G"
  },
  {
    "start": 5,
    "end": 9,
    "fragment": "CUUAA"
  }
]

Checking the answer. The fragments must reflect both the cleavage rule and the requested accessibility setting. Experimental digestion efficiency is not part of the score.

Match an RNA guiderna.guide_hitsGiven an RNA guide and a CDS-derived RNA, find target intervals complementary to the guide within an allowed mismatch count.

Match an RNA guide

Guide-directed recognition is real biology: Argonaute proteins use guide RNAs to recognize complementary mRNA in RNA silencing. The two RNAs pair in opposite directions, so compare target windows with the reverse complement of the supplied 5′→3′ guide.

Examine every target window as long as the guide. Count unequal positions and retain windows at or below the given maximum. This is a simplified sequence screen: real guide systems distinguish mismatch positions and structural contexts, while this task uses a uniform mismatch count with no gaps or wobble.

Role in related tasks

Complementary-hit screening helps identify candidate RNA probes or target-site changes. Probe selection uses the hits for sequence discrimination, and guide-escape design uses them to disrupt a specified interaction. Broader oligonucleotide design methods also model binding thermodynamics and competing structures.

Method reference: NUPACK documentation.

Example

Inputs. Coding RNA AUG GCU GGU UAA; 5′→3′ guide AGCC; at most one mismatch.

Procedure. Reverse-complement the guide to get expected target GGCU. Slide a four-base window along the RNA and count unequal positions. GGCU at 3–6 has zero mismatches; GGUU at 7–10 has one. Reject every window with more than one.

Result. [(3,6,0), (7,10,1)], reporting target intervals and mismatch counts.

Final answer:

[
  {
    "target_start": 3,
    "target_end": 6,
    "mismatches": 0
  },
  {
    "target_start": 7,
    "target_end": 10,
    "mismatches": 1
  }
]

Checking the answer. Return all qualifying intervals and their mismatch counts. Sequence compatibility does not establish cellular guide activity.

Answer format and selection · json+

output_format = json

  • Return JSON only after the final-answer marker: exactly the named fields, correct JSON types, and no additional fields or duplicate object keys. Object-key order and insignificant JSON whitespace do not matter.

Count coding-RNA patternsrna.motif_countsTranscribe the CDS and count occurrences of specified short RNA sequences, including overlapping occurrences.

Count coding-RNA patterns

The question supplies literal RNA patterns to measure, such as a two-base sequence or a longer recognition pattern. No recognition motif needs to be inferred from biological context.

Check every possible RNA starting position for each pattern. Include matches crossing codon boundaries, and report a count of zero when a supplied pattern is absent. This gives a simple measurement that synonymous-design tasks can control.

Role in related tasks

A pattern can be a probe’s exact complementary target sequence; counting it measures how many such candidate sites are present. Probe selection adds comparison RNAs, while motif control changes the count through synonymous recoding. Arbitrary patterns have no biological interpretation until a recognition process or experiment is named.

Method reference: NUPACK documentation.

Example

Inputs. Coding RNA AUG GCG CGU UAA; patterns CG, CGCG, and AAA.

Procedure. For each pattern, compare at every possible start, advancing one base at a time. CG starts at 5 and 7; CGCG starts at 5; AAA never occurs. Include matches crossing codon boundaries and include requested zero counts.

Result. {CG:2, CGCG:1, AAA:0}.

Final answer:

{
  "AAA": 0,
  "CG": 2,
  "CGCG": 1
}

Checking the answer. Each supplied pattern must have its exact occurrence count, including overlaps.

Score a specified RNA structurerna.structure_scoreGiven a coding RNA, a pairing map, and numerical pair scores, calculate the score of that particular structure.

Score a specified RNA structure

Both the structure and its scoring table are supplied. The task therefore does not require finding a fold or knowing which structure is most stable in a cell.

First check that every listed pair is allowed and that no base is assigned two partners. If valid, add the supplied score for each pair. Return INVALID if the map violates those conditions. The additive score is a declared toy objective, not thermodynamic free energy.

Exercise scope

RNA base pairing is physical, but the numerical bonuses in this task are supplied exercise scores. Joint RNA-and-codon optimization uses them as an exactly checkable constraint. Practical methods such as LinearDesign use thermodynamic energy models that include stacking and loops, rather than assigning an arbitrary bonus to each isolated pair.

Method reference: LinearDesign.

Example

Inputs. Coding RNA AUG GCU UAA; pairs (1,7) and (3,5); supplied scores AU/UA = 2 and CG/GC = 3.

Procedure. Check that no position is reused and every pair is canonical. Pair 1–7 is A–U, worth 2; pair 3–5 is G–C, worth 3. Add the scores for this supplied map only.

Result. Total score 5. An incompatible or reused base would instead make the result INVALID.

Final answer:

5

Checking the answer. The validity judgement and, when valid, the total must be exact.

Find a maximum-pair RNA foldrna.max_pair_foldFind a noncrossing arrangement of complementary base pairs in a CDS-derived RNA, with as many pairs as possible.

Find a maximum-pair RNA fold

Choose which positions in the coding RNA pair with each other. Pairing means complementary bases: A with U, or C with G; G–U wobble is excluded. Each base can have at most one partner, pairs cannot cross, and paired positions must satisfy the supplied minimum-loop value.

Two stretches of the same RNA align in opposite directions. In an uninterrupted stem, the second stretch is the reverse complement of the first when both are written 5′→3′. For example, 5′-GGA-3′ aligns with 3′-CCU-5′; writing that partner 5′→3′ gives UCC. Bulges or other unpaired bases can interrupt this relationship.

The minimum-loop value is the number of positions that must lie between the endpoints of any pair. Search for the largest possible number of pairs under these rules and return a dot-bracket representation. This is a small algorithmic folding model, not a claim about the RNA’s physical structure.

Exercise scope

This follows the historical Nussinov approach to RNA folding: choose compatible, noncrossing base pairs by combining solutions for shorter sequence segments. The backbone geometry motivates restrictions on very short loops. Maximizing pair count is a deliberate simplification; thermodynamic methods additionally account for stacking and loop energies.

Method references: Nussinov and colleagues: Algorithms for Loop Matchings, ViennaRNA.

Example

Inputs. Coding RNA AUG GCU UAA; minimum enclosed loop length = 3.

Procedure. List canonical pairs with at least three positions between their endpoints. The possibilities are (1,6), (1,7), (2,8), and (2,9). No two can coexist without crossing or reusing a position, so one pair is optimal. A general solver compares the best compatible choices for shorter intervals before combining them. Compare the optimal annotations in ASCII order, with ( before ) before .; the pair 1–6 gives the first annotation.

Result. (....)..., pairing positions 1 and 6. All four allowed single-pair folds have the optimal count, but this one wins the required tie-break.

Final answer:

(....)...

Checking the answer. The structure must have the maximum allowed pair count and be the first optimal dot-bracket string under the declared ASCII order.

output_format = scalar

Selection. Maximize the allowed pair count first. Among optimal structures, choose the ASCII-lexicographically smallest full dot-bracket string, comparing characters in the order opening parenthesis, closing parenthesis, then dot.

TaskDescriptionExpand details
Rewrite with a specified number of DNA changesdesign.synonymous_distanceRewrite a CDS to encode the same protein while changing a requested number of DNA positions.

Rewrite with a specified number of DNA changes

The question supplies a CDS and a permitted range for the number of changed bases. This range is the edit budget: it counts DNA positions whose letters differ between the original and rewritten sequences, not the number of codons touched.

Use synonymous codons to satisfy that range while keeping the complete protein unchanged. The first and terminal stop codons stay fixed, and no bases may be inserted or deleted. This isolates how much DNA sequence can change without changing the encoded product.

Exercise scope

An exact number of DNA changes has no inherent biological benefit. The useful component is enforcing an edit budget while preserving a protein: joint RNA-and-codon optimization uses that constraint while pursuing a separate sequence-design objective.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GGT TAA; require exactly one changed DNA base.

Procedure. Try all synonymous glycine codons while keeping ATG and TAA fixed. GGA, GGC, and GGG each differ from GGT by one base and meet the exact-one-change requirement. Compare their full DNA strings in A<C<G<T order; GGA comes first.

Result. ATG GGA TAA is the unique selected answer: one base changes and protein MG is preserved. GGC is feasible but loses the tie-break.

Final answer:

ATGGGATAA

Checking the answer. The changed-position count must lie within the supplied inclusive range, with protein and fixed codons preserved. Select the first feasible DNA string under the stated order; this need not use the fewest edits.

Answer format and selection · scalar+

output_format = scalar

  • Return one uppercase DNA string using A,C,G,T, without spaces, quotes, labels, or a FASTA header.
  • Return the literal token IMPOSSIBLE only if no feasible sequence exists.

Selection. Among all sequences satisfying every condition, return the lexicographically smallest full DNA string, comparing bases in the order A<C<G<T. This is a tie-break among feasible sequences, not a minimum-edit objective.

When there is no result or no feasible design:

NCBI genetic code 11. Read consecutive triples from nucleotide 1 of the 5′→3′ coding strand. The first codon is an annotated initiator: TTG, CTG, ATT, ATC, ATA, ATG, or GTG encodes M there. Rewrite using permitted codons

The question supplies a list of DNA codons that may be used at internal protein-coding positions. This can model removing selected codons from a construct while leaving the amino-acid sequence intact.

For each internal residue, choose an allowed codon that encodes the same amino acid. Keep the first and terminal stop codons unchanged. If a required amino acid has no permitted encoding at a necessary position, report that the requested rewrite is impossible.

Practical context

DNA Chisel can exclude codons that are rare in a chosen host. That provides a concrete source for an allowlist: retain the other synonymous codons while preserving the protein. The host reference or design policy must be supplied; an excluded codon is not intrinsically undesirable in every organism.

Method reference: DNA Chisel specifications.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GGT TAA; internal-codon allowlist {GGC}.

Procedure. Translate the internal codon to G. Intersect its synonymous codons {GGA,GGC,GGG,GGT} with the allowlist, leaving GGC. Repeat that intersection at every internal position; any empty intersection makes the task impossible.

Result. ATG GGC TAA. If the allowlist contained no glycine codon, return IMPOSSIBLE.

Final answer:

ATGGGCTAA

Checking the answer. Every internal codon must be allowed, and the complete protein must remain identical. The selected sequence must also satisfy the declared tie-break.

Optimize supplied codon preferencesdesign.codon_preferenceChoose synonymous internal codons to maximize a supplied codon-preference score while retaining the protein.

Optimize supplied codon preferences

The question provides positive numerical weights for codons. These are the preference system for this particular instance; there is no need to infer a host’s preferences or predict expression.

For each internal sense position, choose a synonymous codon to maximize the defined codon adaptation index. The first and terminal stop codons are fixed. This simple version has no additional structure or motif constraints; those enter explicitly in compositions.

Practical context

This is the design counterpart of codon adaptation measurement: choose synonymous codons according to a host-derived preference reference when preparing a gene for expression. The joint-design composition adds an RNA constraint; methods such as LinearDesign extend that idea using a thermodynamic folding objective.

Method reference: LinearDesign.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GGT TAA; glycine weights GGA = 0.6, GGC = 1.0, GGG = 0.2, GGT = 0.4.

Procedure. List the synonymous choices and select the greatest supplied weight: GGC at 1.0. With no other constraints, make that choice independently at every internal position; maximizing each positive factor maximizes their geometric mean. If weights tie at a position, choose the first DNA codon in A<C<G<T order.

Result. ATG GGC TAA, with CAI 1.0 for its single included codon.

Final answer:

ATGGGCTAA

Checking the answer. The candidate must encode the original protein and achieve the highest possible score. The selected sequence must also satisfy the declared tie-break.

Match positional codon-preference rangesdesign.codon_profileRewrite internal codons so each position meets its own supplied codon-preference range, while preserving the protein.

Match positional codon-preference ranges

A single whole-CDS average does not specify where high- or low-preference codons occur. This task instead supplies preference weights and a separate acceptable weight interval for each internal codon position.

Choose a synonymous codon whose weight lies inside that position’s interval. A request can deliberately retain lower-preference positions rather than optimizing every position upward. The ranges are supplied design targets, not something the model must infer from a natural expression pattern.

Practical context

Codon harmonization methods, such as CHARMING, try to reproduce a local pattern of codon usage when adapting a gene to another host, rather than maximizing every codon’s preference. The supplied positional ranges make that design idea testable here; they are a codon-usage proxy, not measured translation speeds.

Method reference: CHARMING.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GGT GGT TAA; weights GGA = 0.6, GGC = 1.0, GGG = 0.2, GGT = 0.4; internal-position weight ranges [0.3,0.5] then [0.8,1.0].

Procedure. At the first internal glycine, keep only synonymous codons with weights in 0.3–0.5: GGT. At the second, keep those in 0.8–1.0: GGC. Check each position against its own range, rather than maximizing every weight.

Result. ATG GGT GGC TAA, preserving protein MGG.

Final answer:

ATGGGTGGCTAA

Checking the answer. Every positional interval must be satisfied, with the protein and terminal codons preserved. Report IMPOSSIBLE if no assignment exists.

Control local GC by recodingdesign.gc_windowsSynonymously rewrite a CDS so every local DNA window has GC content within a supplied range.

Control local GC by recoding

The question gives a window length and a minimum and maximum GC fraction. These define local composition requirements rather than a single whole-gene target.

Change internal codons without changing the protein, then check every full window one base at a time across the final DNA. Overlapping windows couple the choices: fixing one region can create a problem in its neighbor. The first and terminal stop codons remain fixed.

Practical context

Synthetic-gene design often needs to reduce local GC extremes while keeping the encoded product fixed. The cloning-and-GC composition combines this requirement with restriction-site removal, reflecting the simultaneous sequence constraints handled by practical construct-design tools.

Method references: Twist gene-design resources, DNA Chisel examples.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GGG TAA; six-base windows must have GC fraction from 1/3 through 1/2.

Procedure. The original windows have G/C counts 4,4,4,3; permitted counts are 2 or 3. Test all synonymous glycine codons and every window of each full candidate. GGA and GGT both give counts 3,3,3,2. Compare their DNA strings and choose GGA first.

Result. ATG GGA TAA satisfies every window, preserves MG, and is the first feasible DNA string.

Final answer:

ATGGGATAA

Checking the answer. The same final CDS must pass every window and preserve the original protein. A good average GC value alone is insufficient.

Used in: Remove cloning sites while controlling GC

Remove specified DNA motifsdesign.remove_dna_motifsRemove every occurrence of specified DNA patterns using synonymous changes, preserving the encoded protein.

Remove specified DNA motifs

A construct may contain a recognition site for an enzyme that will be used during cloning. For example, EcoRI recognizes GAATTC, the site in the worked example. The question supplies the unwanted patterns and whether to search the coding strand alone or both strands.

Change internal codons synonymously until every forbidden occurrence is absent from the final CDS. Search across codon boundaries as well as within codons, and check that the edits did not create a new copy elsewhere. Preserve the first and terminal stop codons.

Practical context

Golden Gate assembly requires removing unwanted internal recognition sites for the Type IIS enzyme being used; otherwise the insert can be cut internally. This synonymous cleanup is often called domestication. The combined design task also controls GC while removing the sites.

Method reference: GoldenMutagenesis domestication.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GAA TTC TGA; forbidden forward-strand pattern GAATTC.

Procedure. Find GAATTC at bases 4–9. Enumerate synonymous E/F encodings and rescan each full CDS. GAA TTC is forbidden, while GAA TTT is allowed. It sorts before the also-valid GAG TTC and GAG TTT; keep the original first and stop codons.

Result. ATG GAA TTT TGA removes the site and preserves MEF. The F-codon change is the canonical choice here; changing the E codon would also work but sorts later.

Final answer:

ATGGAATTTTGA

Checking the answer. The candidate must preserve the protein and contain no forbidden hits under the requested strand rule. The selected sequence must also satisfy the declared tie-break.
