Introduce a DNA recognition sitedesign.insert_dna_motifCreate a specified DNA recognition sequence at a requested CDS position through synonymous changes.

Introduce a DNA recognition site

A restriction-enzyme recognition site can be introduced as a marker for screening an engineered sequence. The worked example uses EcoRI’s real GAATTC site. The input specifies the literal recognition sequence and the DNA position where it must begin.

Choose synonymous internal codons so the required bases appear at the requested location, even if the site spans several codons. Other copies of the site are allowed in this version. Keep the first and terminal stop codons fixed.

Practical context

Introducing a synonymous restriction site can create a convenient way to screen an engineered allele by restriction digestion. This task isolates site creation without changing the protein. Motif scanning can then confirm where the recognition sequence occurs.

Method reference: Restriction-site markers in engineered alleles.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GAG TTC TGA; require literal pattern GAATTC starting at DNA position 4.

Procedure. Compare the requested six bases with positions 4–9, currently GAGTTC. Change GAG→GAA, a synonymous E codon, and leave TTC unchanged. Check the full requested interval and the translated protein.

Result. ATG GAA TTC TGA, containing GAATTC at [4,9] and still encoding MEF.

Final answer:

ATGGAATTCTGA

Checking the answer. The required site must appear at the specified start and all protein-preservation conditions must hold. Otherwise return IMPOSSIBLE.

Break homopolymers and repeatsdesign.break_repeatsUse synonymous substitutions to remove overly long runs of one base and excessive repeated DNA substrings.

Break homopolymers and repeats

The question gives the longest permitted run of identical bases and limits on how many times a substring of a given length may occur. These are sequence-design requirements supplied for the instance.

Recode internal codons without changing the protein. Count runs and repeated substrings across the entire final CDS, including codon junctions and overlapping occurrences. The first and terminal stop codons cannot be changed.

Practical context

Long homopolymers and repeated sequences can make DNA synthesis and amplification more difficult. Synonymous recoding can reduce that sequence complexity without changing the protein. The benchmark’s explicit repeat rules represent one part of the broader manufacturability screening used by synthesis providers.

Method reference: Twist gene-design resources.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG AAA AAA TAA; maximum identical-base run = 2; every three-base substring may occur at most twice.

Procedure. The six consecutive A bases fail the run limit. Try the lysine alternatives AAA/AAG at both internal positions. AAG at each breaks the run; then count all overlapping three-base substrings across the complete result.

Result. ATG AAG AAG TAA: maximum run 2, no three-base substring occurs more than twice, and protein MKK is preserved.

Final answer:

ATGAAGAAGTAA

Checking the answer. Every repeat limit must hold on the final sequence while translation stays unchanged. Satisfying only the homopolymer limit is not enough when substring limits are also supplied.

Control coding-RNA motifsdesign.rna_motif_controlSynonymously rewrite DNA so its coding RNA contains specified numbers of supplied RNA patterns.

Control coding-RNA motifs

The patterns are RNA strings using U, and each comes with an acceptable minimum and maximum number of occurrences. This can request removing a pattern, introducing one, or controlling its copy count.

Choose synonymous DNA codons, transcribe the candidate, and count each RNA pattern in that final RNA. Include overlapping matches and matches crossing codon boundaries. Keep the protein and first and terminal stop codons unchanged.

Exercise scope

If a supplied pattern is a probe’s exact complementary target, synonymous recoding can remove that candidate binding sequence while preserving the protein. Guide-escape design extends this idea to near-matches. Dinucleotide control provides another concrete composition target; a generic unnamed pattern remains an abstract constraint.

Method reference: NUPACK documentation.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GGT TAA; coding RNA must contain exactly zero GGU patterns and exactly one GGC pattern.

Procedure. Try synonymous glycine codons, transcribe each candidate, and count the requested patterns at every RNA position. GGT→GGC removes the GGU occurrence and creates one GGC occurrence.

Result. ATG GGC TAA gives RNA AUG GGC UAA, counts {GGU:0, GGC:1}, and unchanged protein MG.

Final answer:

ATGGGCTAA

Checking the answer. All pattern counts must fall within their supplied ranges on the same final RNA, while the encoded protein is preserved.

Control RNA dinucleotide countsdesign.dinucleotide_countsSynonymously rewrite a CDS to meet requested counts of adjacent RNA-base pairs such as CG or UA.

Control RNA dinucleotide counts

A dinucleotide is simply two consecutive bases along a sequence, not a structural base pair. CpG means a C followed by G; UpA means U followed by A. The question gives acceptable counts for selected RNA dinucleotides.

Change synonymous DNA codons and count adjacent pairs in the resulting coding RNA at every position. A pair spanning two codons counts just like a pair inside a codon. Keep the protein and first and terminal stop codons fixed.

Practical context

Dinucleotide composition can affect how cellular factors recognize RNA; for example, ZAP recognizes CpG-containing RNA. A controlled synonymous panel uses count changes to construct testable comparisons while preserving protein identity and total GC. The count is an experimental design variable, rather than a prediction of an effect’s size.

Method reference: Origin and evolution of the zinc finger antiviral protein.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GCT GGT TAA; require exactly one RNA CG and exactly one RNA GC.

Procedure. Enumerate synonymous alanine/glycine codons and transcribe each candidate. Count every adjacent CG and GC, including codon junctions. GCC GGA is the first DNA combination with exactly one of each: GC at positions 4–5 and CG at the codon junction, positions 6–7.

Result. ATG GCC GGA TAA is the first feasible DNA string; coding-RNA counts are CG=1 and GC=1, and the protein is MAG.

Final answer:

ATGGCCGGATAA

Checking the answer. Every requested dinucleotide count must lie within its stated range in the final coding RNA.

Repair pairing synonymouslydesign.pairing_repairUse synonymous CDS changes to make specified positions in its coding RNA form allowed base pairs.

Repair pairing synonymously

The question supplies the intended RNA pairs and the DNA positions that may be edited. A mismatch in the supplied map is known in advance; the model does not have to discover the structure or identify a biological compensatory mutation.

Choose changes at the permitted positions so every listed RNA pair becomes canonical, while the CDS still encodes its original protein. The first and terminal stop codons remain fixed. A change that repairs one pair but changes an amino acid is not a valid repair here.

Practical context

This has a direct experimental precedent: a study of bacterial rpsT mRNA found that some fitness costs of synonymous mutations could be compensated by second synonymous changes restoring predicted base pairing. Repair and verification isolates the sequence-design logic: restore the proposed RNA contact without changing the encoded protein.

Method reference: Synonymous mutations and restoration of mRNA base pairing.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GGG TAA; required RNA pair (3,6); only DNA position 6 may change.

Procedure. Transcription gives G at both positions 3 and 6, an incompatible G–G pair. Try synonymous glycine codons at the editable position: GGG→GGC puts C at RNA position 6. Recheck the G–C pair and compare the encoded proteins.

Result. ATG GGC TAA restores canonical G–C pairing at (3,6) and preserves MG.

Final answer:

ATGGGCTAA

Checking the answer. All specified pairs must be compatible, all DNA changes permitted, and the protein unchanged. The selected sequence must also satisfy the declared tie-break.

Optimize a fixed RNA pairing scoredesign.structure_scoreChoose synonymous codons to maximize or minimize a supplied score for a fixed coding-RNA pairing map.

Optimize a fixed RNA pairing score

The RNA position pairs are fixed by the question. A numerical table assigns values to allowed pair types, and the question says whether to make their total larger or smaller. This is not a request to predict folding free energy.

Search synonymous versions of the CDS, preserving the first and terminal stop codons. Every required pair must remain canonical. Among feasible candidates, choose one whose total pair score is optimal in the requested direction.

Exercise scope

This is an optimization exercise over a supplied map and artificial pair scores. The joint-design composition tests whether the solver can satisfy that objective alongside codon and edit constraints. Practical mRNA design uses richer folding objectives, as illustrated by LinearDesign.

Method reference: LinearDesign.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GGA GGT TAA; pair (6,9); scores AU/UA = 2 and CG/GC = 3; maximize the score.

Procedure. Each glycine has four synonymous codons, so examine 4×4 choices. Keep only candidates whose RNA bases 6 and 9 form AU, UA, CG, or GC. Score those four possibilities; CG and GC attain the largest supplied value, 3. Break the equal score by DNA order: GGC GGG precedes GGG GGC.

Result. ATG GGC GGG TAA is optimal: RNA positions 6 and 9 are C–G, score 3, and protein MGG is unchanged.

Final answer:

ATGGGCGGGTAA

Checking the answer. The final CDS must preserve the protein, satisfy every pair, and attain the optimum under the supplied score table.

Disrupt a specified local hairpindesign.expose_rna_windowSynonymously change a CDS to break specified RNA stem pairs that involve a selected region.

Disrupt a specified local hairpin

The question supplies a candidate pairing map, an RNA interval of interest, and the DNA positions that may change. It asks for disruption of the listed stem pairs touching that region, rather than discovery of all possible alternative structures.

Make permitted synonymous substitutions so every relevant listed pair becomes incompatible under the no-wobble pairing rule. Pairs outside the selected region need not be broken. Preserve the protein and fixed terminal codons.

Exercise scope

A complementary probe must compete with bases already paired inside its target RNA. Disrupting a proposed stem is therefore a first step toward designing an accessible binding region. Practical methods also evaluate alternative folds and binding energies; this task checks only the supplied contacts.

Method reference: NUPACK documentation.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GGC TAA; candidate stem pair (3,6); target RNA interval [6,6]; only DNA base 6 may change.

Procedure. The listed pair touches the target and currently contains G–C. Only base 6 may change. Among synonymous glycine choices, GGA, GGG, and GGT all make that pair noncanonical under the no-wobble rule. GGA comes first in DNA order.

Result. ATG GGA TAA changes the listed pair to G–A and preserves MG. It is selected before the other feasible encodings; alternative folds are not evaluated.

Final answer:

ATGGGATAA

Checking the answer. All targeted listed pairs must be broken without an unauthorized DNA or protein change. Passing does not establish physical accessibility if the RNA can adopt an unlisted fold.

Create a guide-escape controldesign.guide_escapeCreate a synonymous CDS whose coding RNA no longer closely matches a supplied RNA guide.

Create a guide-escape control

The question supplies a guide, permitted DNA-edit locations, and the minimum number of mismatches required between that guide and every potential RNA target window. This can define a matched sequence-recognition control that encodes the same protein.

Change only permitted DNA positions using synonymous choices, then compare every same-length RNA window with the guide’s reverse complement. The mismatch minimum must hold everywhere, so removing the original best match must not create another close match nearby. Keep the terminal codons fixed.

Practical context

Synonymous changes are used to make RNAi-resistant rescue constructs: the same protein is reintroduced from RNA that escapes the knockdown reagent, helping test whether a phenotype came from loss of that protein. The matched-target composition captures the sequence-design step; reagent activity still requires experimental testing.

Method reference: RNAi-resistant rescue in a B-cyclin study.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GCT TAA; RNA guide AGCC; at least one mismatch required in every four-base target window; only DNA position 6 may change.

Procedure. The guide’s reverse complement is GGCU, an exact match at RNA positions 3–6. Enumerate synonymous changes at DNA base 6 and check every four-base RNA window. GCA, GCC, and GCG all remove every perfect target; GCA sorts first.

Result. ATG GCA TAA preserves MA and meets the mismatch minimum in every window. GCC also passes but is not the selected answer.

Final answer:

ATGGCATAA

Checking the answer. The candidate must preserve the protein and meet the mismatch minimum at every window. The task makes no claim about actual resistance to an RNA-targeting reagent.

A synonymous codon change substitutes a codon with another codon encoding the same amino acid. A synonymous CDS rewrite preserves the complete translated protein, length, first codon, and terminal stop codon; no insertions/deletions or new stops. Keep the first and last codons unchanged. Codon boundaries begin at nucleotide 1. Constraints must also be checked across neighboring codon boundaries.

Coding RNA uses A,C,G,U. Canonical Watson–Crick pairs are A–U, U–A, C–G, G–C. This benchmark excludes G–U wobble unless the named rule set explicitly includes it. A pairing map lists 1-based positions (i,j) on the same RNA. In dot-bracket notation, matching parentheses pair their positions and dots are unpaired. A hairpin consists of paired stem positions enclosing an unpaired loop. Pair compatibility alone does not establish the physical fold.

A coding DNA strand is written 5′→3′. Its coding RNA has the same order of bases with U in place of T. The opposite strand is antiparallel. DNA complement: A↔T, C↔G. A reverse complement complements every base and reverses the sequence.

This is a tie-break among feasible sequences, not a minimum-edit objective.

Build a controlled synonymous paneldesign.variant_panelGenerate several synonymous CDSs with different requested RNA CG counts but the same total number of G/C bases.

Build a controlled synonymous panel

The question asks for a matched collection, not one optimized sequence. Every member must encode the original protein. Each has its own target number of adjacent CG occurrences in coding RNA, while all share one required total G+C count.

Choose distinct synonymous sequences satisfying those counts exactly. This creates a simple controlled comparison: CG occurrence count varies while protein identity and overall GC composition are held fixed. It does not claim to hold every other RNA property constant.

Practical context

Matched synonymous panels let experiments compare RNA abundance or protein output while keeping the encoded protein fixed. Here CG count is the intended variable and total GC is additionally controlled. The audit composition verifies those properties; it does not assume other RNA features remain identical.

Method reference: Coding-sequence determinants of expression.

Example

Inputs. Reference CDS ATG GCT GGC TAA; two requested RNA CG counts [0,1]; each panel member must contain exactly 6 G/C bases.

Procedure. Enumerate complete pairs of distinct synonymous CDSs in the requested CG-count order, retaining only members with six G/C bases. For the zero-CG slot, GCA GGC is the earliest feasible internal encoding. For the one-CG slot, GCC GGA comes first. Compare whole panels by the first differing DNA string.

Result. Panel ["ATGGCAGGCTAA","ATGGCCGGATAA"]: CG counts are [0,1], G/C counts are [6,6], and both encode MAG. This is the first complete feasible panel, not two arbitrarily chosen witnesses.

Final answer:

["ATGGCAGGCTAA","ATGGCCGGATAA"]

Checking the answer. Every member must meet its assigned CG count and the common GC count, and all must preserve the protein and terminal codons.

TaskDescriptionExpand details
Encode a requested amino-acid substitutionconstruct.minimal_aa_editChange one requested protein residue by replacing its DNA codon with as few base substitutions as possible.

Encode a requested amino-acid substitution

The question identifies an internal residue and the amino acid it should become. Unlike synonymous redesign, this task deliberately changes the protein at that one position.

Consider codons encoding the requested amino acid and choose the one differing from the original codon at the fewest bases. Only that codon may change. If several choices use the same number of changes, select the alphabetically first DNA codon.

Practical context

This is the sequence-design part of site-directed mutagenesis: encode a chosen amino-acid replacement with as few nucleotide substitutions as possible. The protein-editing and cloning composition also removes unwanted assembly sites, turning the residue-level request into a more usable construct sequence.

Method reference: Site-directed mutagenesis protocol.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GGT TAA; replace residue 2, G, with D.

Procedure. List D codons GAT and GAC. Compare each with original GGT: GAT changes one base, while GAC changes two. Choose the smallest change count, using DNA alphabetical order only if counts tie.

Result. ATG GAT TAA, encoding MD, with one changed DNA base.

Final answer:

ATGGATTAA

Checking the answer. The intended residue must change, every other base must stay fixed, and the chosen codon must satisfy the minimum-change and tie-breaking rules.

Remove a protein motifconstruct.remove_peptide_motifModify permitted protein residues to remove a specified peptide pattern, then return DNA encoding the modified product.

Remove a protein motif

The question supplies an unwanted literal amino-acid sequence and a list of protein positions that may change, with the allowed replacement residues at each position. It does not ask which natural mutations would preserve function.

Choose permitted amino-acid changes until the unwanted pattern is absent from the complete protein. Encode that product in a CDS while retaining its first and terminal stop codons. A change can remove one occurrence but create another, so the final product must be checked globally.

Practical context

An unwanted protease recognition sequence can interfere with processing an engineered protein. This task removes a specified motif under explicit amino-acid permissions. Motif-to-DNA mapping identifies the encoding codons; the allowed changes must be chosen by the experiment, since motif removal alone cannot establish preserved protein function.

Method reference: ExPASy PeptideCutter.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG AAA AAA TAA, encoding MKK; forbid KK; residue 2 may be K or R, while other residues stay fixed.

Procedure. Try the permitted K/R choices at residue 2. Keeping K leaves the forbidden KK, so choose R and preserve every other residue. Enumerate DNA encodings of MRK with fixed first/stop codons. AGA is the first arginine codon and AAA the first lysine codon in DNA order.

Result. ATG AGA AAA TAA, encoding MRK. The earlier CGT example encodes the same valid protein but loses the DNA tie-break.

Final answer:

ATGAGAAAATAA

Checking the answer. The resulting protein must obey every residue permission and contain no forbidden pattern. Retained activity or folding is not part of this task.

Build a tagged protein CDSconstruct.tag_fusionAssemble a CDS encoding a supplied tag and linker at a specified end of the original protein.

Build a tagged protein CDS

A tag is a supplied coding module added to a protein construct, often to support purification or detection. The question gives the DNA for the tag and linker, so the model does not invent their sequences.

Follow the explicit assembly convention. For an N-terminal tag, retain the original initiating codon, then add tag and linker before the remaining original sense codons. For a C-terminal tag, append linker and tag after the original sense codons. Keep one final stop.

Practical context

A concrete affinity tag is His6: six histidines that bind nickel affinity material, allowing the attached protein to be captured during purification. The supplied tag and linker DNA encode such modules. The tag-cleavage composition follows a removable tag through processing and calculates the resulting product masses.

Method reference: His6-tagged protein purification.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GCT TAA; His6 tag DNA CAT CAT CAT CAT CAT CAT; linker GGT encodes G; placement = N.

Procedure. Keep the original ATG, append the six-histidine tag and linker, then append the original sense sequence after ATG and its stop. Following the supplied placement convention gives M + HHHHHH + G + A.

Result. ATG CAT CAT CAT CAT CAT CAT GGT GCT TAA, encoding MHHHHHHGA.

Final answer:

ATGCATCATCATCATCATCATGGTGCTTAA

Checking the answer. The constructed DNA must contain the modules in the required order and preserve their reading frame, with no unintended sequence changes.

Used in: Build a tagged construct, cleave it, measure products

Derive TEV-cleaved productsconstruct.tev_productsTranslate a constructed CDS and determine the protein fragments remaining after the specified TEV cleavage.

Derive TEV-cleaved products

TEV protease is a real enzyme derived from tobacco etch virus and widely used to remove engineered affinity tags. ENLYFQG is a common cleavage-site sequence; the cut is ENLYFQ|G. The benchmark fixes this exact site even though the actual enzyme accepts some additional sequences.

Locate all complete recognition sites and split the protein at their cleavage bonds. The G belongs to the downstream fragment. Return every fragment in its original order rather than automatically discarding the tag or reporting only a preferred product.

Practical context

TEV protease is used to remove affinity tags after protein purification. Predicting the products establishes what tag sequence or cleavage scar remains on the target. The cleavage-and-mass composition uses those exact sequences when deriving an expected identity readout.

Method reference: Removal of affinity tags with TEV protease.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GAA AAT CTG TAT TTT CAG GGT GCT TAA, encoding MENLYFQGA.

Procedure. Scan for the complete ENLYFQG pattern. It occupies residues 2–8; cut after its Q at residue 7. Keep all residues, with the G at residue 8 on the downstream side.

Result. Ordered fragments [MENLYFQ, GA].

Final answer:

["MENLYFQ","GA"]

Checking the answer. The fragments must reconstruct the original protein when joined and place each cleavage at the stated bond.

Enumerate a degenerate codon librarylibrary.codon_productsExpand an ambiguous internal DNA codon and count how many concrete codons encode each amino acid or stop.

Enumerate a degenerate codon library

Degenerate oligonucleotide synthesis mixes nucleotide choices at selected positions, producing a pool of DNA sequences for mutagenesis experiments. IUPAC notation describes those choices compactly: N, for example, permits A/C/G/T. The question asks which protein alternatives such a mixed codon covers at one CDS position.

Expand all possible base combinations and translate each codon internally. Count concrete codons per amino acid, rather than reporting each amino acid once. These are combinatorial counts, not measured library frequencies or expression levels.

Practical context

Before ordering a degenerate oligonucleotide, library designers need to know which amino acids it covers, how redundantly it encodes them, and whether it includes stops. Library design and verification uses this enumeration to audit a proposed mixed-codon design.

Method reference: SwiftLib.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GCN TAA; enumerate internal codon 2, where N = A/C/G/T.

Procedure. Expand GCN to GCA, GCC, GCG, and GCT. Translate each and increment its product’s count once: all four give A. Keep codon multiplicity here, unlike the distinct-outcome set task.

Result. {A:4}. This counts four concrete codons, not an experimentally measured abundance.

Final answer:

{
  "A": 4
}

Checking the answer. The residue and stop counts must account for every concrete codon in the expansion exactly once.

Each uppercase one-letter amino-acid key counts how many concrete codons encode it; STOP counts concrete stop codons.
  • Include every produced outcome, including unintended amino acids and stops. Omit zero counts. Values are positive integers, not probabilities or counts in the whole protein. Their sum equals the number of concrete codons in the expansion.

Used in: Design a codon library and verify its coverage

Design a focused degenerate codonlibrary.design_codonChoose an ambiguous DNA codon that covers requested amino acids without encoding stops, while limiting unwanted alternatives.

Design a focused degenerate codon

The question supplies the amino acids desired at one internal CDS position. One IUPAC triplet may cover those choices compactly, but its expansion can also include additional amino acids.

Search triplets whose concrete codons cover every requested residue and none of the stops. Prefer the fewest extra amino-acid types, then the fewest concrete codons. A final alphabetical tie-break makes the answer unique. If no triplet can satisfy stop-free coverage, return IMPOSSIBLE.

Practical context

Focused mutagenesis libraries target selected amino acids while limiting how many variants must be screened. Degenerate-codon optimization tools such as SwiftLib address that trade-off. The design-and-audit composition checks the resulting codon mixture’s actual coverage instead of relying on its intended target set.

Method reference: SwiftLib.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GAT TAA; redesign internal codon 2 to cover target residues {D,E}.

Procedure. Enumerate IUPAC triplets, reject any with a stop, and rank by extra residue types, concrete-codon count, then ASCII triplet order. GAK expands to GAG (E) and GAT (D), with zero extras and the minimum possible two codons. Among tied two-codon solutions, GAK sorts first.

Result. GAK, where K means G or T. Its expansion covers exactly D and E without a stop.

Final answer:

GAK

Checking the answer. Coverage and stop avoidance are mandatory. The answer must also achieve the declared ordering of the optimization criteria.

output_format = scalar

Selection. Require target-residue coverage and no stops. Minimize extra amino-acid types, then the number of concrete codons, then the IUPAC triplet in ASCII order A<B<C<D<G<H<K<M<N<R<S<T<V<W<Y. Compare the symbols themselves, not their expanded nucleotide sets.

When there is no result or no feasible design:

Delete a protein intervalconstruct.inframe_deletionRemove a specified range of protein residues by deleting exactly the corresponding complete DNA codons.

Delete a protein interval

The question identifies an internal residue interval in the protein encoded by a CDS. The goal is to remove that segment without shifting the grouping of downstream codons.

Map the residue interval to DNA, delete those complete codons, and leave all other DNA unchanged. The interval excludes the initiating residue, and the original terminal stop is retained.

Practical context

Deletion constructs can test the contribution of an explicitly chosen protein region. This task turns those residue boundaries into an in-frame DNA deletion. It prepares the sequence for such a comparison; deciding whether the shortened protein still folds or functions requires evidence beyond the deletion operation.

Method reference: Site-directed mutagenesis protocol.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GCT GCT GGT TAA; delete protein residues 2–3.

Procedure. Map the requested residues to DNA bases 4–9, then delete those complete codons. Join the untouched prefix ATG to the untouched suffix GGT TAA. Six removed bases preserve the downstream grouping.

Result. ATG GGT TAA, encoding MG instead of MAAG.

Final answer:

ATGGGTTAA

Checking the answer. Exactly the requested codons must be deleted; synonymous changes elsewhere are not allowed in this task.

Join coding modulesconstruct.join_modulesJoin two supplied CDSs with a coding linker to make one continuous fusion-protein CDS.

Join coding modules

The question gives two complete coding sequences and a linker made of complete, stop-free codons. Joining the DNA naively would retain the first CDS’s stop and prevent translation into the second module.

Remove the first CDS’s terminal stop and the second CDS’s initiating codon. Join the remaining first module, linker, and second module, retaining the first initiator and the second terminal stop. This fixes precisely which residues appear at the junction.

Practical context

Fusion constructs combine a target protein with reporters, tags, or other supplied coding modules. Correct reading frame and stop handling are essential at each join. The junction-audit composition then checks whether assembly created an unwanted peptide motif across a module boundary.

Method reference: Addgene bacterial expression collection.

Example

Inputs. CDS A ATG GCT TAA; CDS B ATG GGT TGA; linker DNA AAA.

Procedure. Remove A’s terminal TAA and B’s initial ATG. Concatenate A’s remaining sense codons, linker AAA, and B’s remaining sequence including its TGA. Translate the assembled DNA to check the join.

Result. ATG GCT AAA GGT TGA, encoding MAKG.

Final answer:

ATGGCTAAAGGTTGA

Checking the answer. The fused DNA must follow that exact junction convention and preserve all remaining module bases.

Design an RNA-editing-dependent productconstruct.edit_aware_encodingDesign a synonymous CDS whose coding RNA produces a requested different protein after explicitly specified RNA edits.

Design an RNA-editing-dependent product

The question supplies an original CDS, fixed RNA editing events, a desired post-edit protein, and the DNA positions that may change. Before editing, the designed DNA must still encode the original protein.

Choose permitted synonymous codons that make those particular RNA edits yield the desired product. Check two branches: translation before editing and translation after transcription plus editing. Editing sites and enzyme behavior are given, not predicted.

Exercise scope

ADAR enzymes convert RNA adenosine to inosine, which is often read as G during translation. The example represents that recoding as A→G and asks for a synonymous DNA encoding with different unedited and edited proteins. This is a two-state sequence exercise: the editing event is assumed, not evidence that ADAR will act at the chosen site.

Method reference: Programmable editing by endogenous ADAR.

Example

Inputs. Reference CDS ATG TCT TAA encodes MS; only DNA bases 4 and 5 may change; the supplied RNA recoding sets position 4 to G; desired edited protein = MG. For this translation-only example, A-to-I editing is represented as A→G.

Procedure. Try synonymous serine encodings reachable at the permitted bases. TCT would become GCT (A) after the edit; AGT becomes GGT (G). Choose AGT: before editing it still encodes S, and its A at RNA position 4 is the supplied editing target.

Result. ATG AGT TAA: unedited protein MS; edited RNA representation AUG GGU UAA, giving MG. The example assumes the recoding; it does not predict enzyme activity.

Final answer:

ATGAGTTAA

Checking the answer. One designed CDS must pass both protein requirements and every DNA-edit restriction. An answer that changes the unedited protein is invalid.

A synonymous codon change substitutes a codon with another codon encoding the same amino acid. A synonymous CDS rewrite preserves the complete translated protein, length, first codon, and terminal stop codon; no insertions/deletions or new stops. Keep the first and last codons unchanged. Codon boundaries begin at nucleotide 1. Constraints must also be checked across neighboring codon boundaries.

A coding DNA strand is written 5′→3′. Its coding RNA has the same order of bases with U in place of T. The opposite strand is antiparallel. DNA complement: A↔T, C↔G. A reverse complement complements every base and reverses the sequence.

Edits use original, 1-based coordinates. A replacement [a,b,text] replaces inclusive interval a..b with text, which may be empty. An insertion at boundary k inserts after original base k (0 means before base 1). Listed edits never overlap and apply simultaneously; later edits are not renumbered. RNA substitutions are specified on the coding RNA after T→U.

Choose CDS-internal PCR primersassay.primer_pairChoose forward and reverse DNA primers for a specified interval entirely within a supplied CDS.

Choose CDS-internal PCR primers

The question fixes the desired amplified interval and primer length. It also supplies acceptable GC fractions. The primers must bind the intended ends in opposing directions; no genomic flanks need to be supplied.

Take the first primer-length bases of the interval for the forward primer. Reverse-complement the last primer-length bases for the reverse primer. Check both composition limits and uniqueness of their intended oriented binding sites within this CDS.

Practical context

Correct primer orientation and target endpoints are prerequisites for amplifying a CDS segment. This task isolates that sequence-selection step. Practical tools such as Primer3 also evaluate melting temperatures, self-complementarity, and interactions between primers when choosing a pair for an assay.

Method reference: Primer3.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GCT TGA; amplicon interval [1,9]; illustrative primer length 4; GC bounds [0.25,0.50].

Procedure. Take the first four interval bases, ATGG, as the forward primer. Reverse-complement its last four bases, TTGA, to obtain TCAA as the reverse primer. Their GC fractions are 2/4 and 1/4, and each intended oriented binding site occurs once in this CDS.

Result. Forward ATGG; reverse TCAA. The short length illustrates the algorithm, not a proposed laboratory primer pair.

Final answer:

{
  "status": "ok",
  "forward": "ATGG",
  "reverse": "TCAA"
}

Checking the answer. Both sequences must have the correct orientation and interval endpoints and satisfy the supplied constraints. Melting behavior and genome-wide specificity are outside this version.

Select a CDS-specific RNA probeassay.select_rna_probeChoose a complementary RNA probe that matches the target CDS’s RNA but differs sufficiently from every supplied background RNA.

Select a CDS-specific RNA probe

The question supplies a target CDS, comparison CDSs, a probe length, and a required minimum mismatch count against backgrounds. This defines specificity relative to a stated panel rather than the whole transcriptome.

Find a target window and take its reverse complement as the probe. Reject it if any same-length background window is too close a match. Among passing probes choose the alphabetically first RNA sequence. Only exact-length, ungapped comparisons are used.

Practical context

RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization detects transcripts using labeled oligonucleotide probes that bind complementary RNA sequences. This task isolates the candidate-specificity screen against supplied CDS-derived RNAs. Binding strength, competing structures, and detection chemistry require additional assay design.

Method references: Imaging individual mRNA molecules with labeled probes, NUPACK documentation.

Example

Inputs. Target CDS ATG GCT TAA; background CDS ATG GGT TAA; probe length 3; require at least one mismatch to every background window.

Procedure. Transcribe both CDSs. Reverse-complement each target window to generate probes, then reject probes with any exact background target. The surviving probes are AAG, AGC, and GCC. Sort those RNA strings alphabetically.

Result. AAG, complementary to target window CUU at positions 5–7. Every background window differs from CUU at least once.

Final answer:

AAG

Checking the answer. The probe must perfectly complement a target window and meet the mismatch minimum everywhere in every background. Report IMPOSSIBLE if no probe qualifies.

  • Return IMPOSSIBLE if no probe meets every requirement.

Distinguish CDSs with a probe panelassay.min_probe_panelSelect the smallest subset of supplied RNA probes whose match patterns distinguish every CDS in a supplied collection.

Distinguish CDSs with a probe panel

Each candidate probe gives a binary measurement: it either has an exact complementary match in a CDS-derived RNA or it does not. Several probes together give each RNA a pattern of positive and negative results.

Choose probes so no two RNAs have the same resulting pattern. Minimize the number chosen; use the specified probe-ID ordering to break ties. This is a measurement-selection problem, not a request to predict hybridization efficiency.

Practical context

Choosing a small set of informative probes can reduce the number of measurements needed to distinguish candidate RNAs. The sequence-to-panel composition supplies the match matrix. This is the combinatorial selection stage, using ideal binary hits rather than measured hybridization performance.

Example

Inputs. Coding RNAs A = AUG GCU UAA, B = AUG GGU UAA, C = AUG GCC UAA; probes p1 = AGC, p2 = ACC, p3 = GGC.

Procedure. Compute exact complementary hits. In probe order p1,p2,p3, signatures are A:100, B:010, C:001. Test subsets in increasing size: no single binary probe distinguishes three RNAs. Two suffice; use the sorted-ID tie-break.

Result. Select [p1,p2], giving A:10, B:01, C:00. The all-zero signature is still distinct in this supplied panel.

Final answer:

["p1","p2"]

Checking the answer. Every RNA must have a unique signature and the panel must use the minimum possible number of probes.

Overlapping reading frames

Explicitly annotated overlaps and coupled constraints.

2 tasks
overlap task definitions
TaskDescriptionExpand details
Evaluate a change in two framesoverlap.compare_productsGiven two annotated coding windows and a DNA substitution, compare the before-and-after peptide in each window.

Evaluate a change in two frames

Overlapping coding information occurs naturally. In the human CDKN2A locus, p16INK4a and p14ARF use different reading frames in a shared exon. One DNA edit can therefore affect two encoded products. Here both coding intervals and strands are supplied; no gene or splice-site discovery is required.

Apply the equal-length DNA replacement and translate each annotated window before and after it. For these windows, use internal codon meanings throughout and retain stops as * rather than truncating: the goal is to expose every codon-level consequence.

Role in related tasks

When two annotated coding windows overlap, a DNA edit can change both products. The overlapping-product audit uses this comparison to check the intended edit and the product that must remain fixed. The windows are supplied; discovering overlapping genes is a different problem.

Example

Inputs. DNA ATG GCT AAA TAA; plus-strand windows A = [4,6] and B = [5,7]; replace base 5, C, with T.

Procedure. Read each annotated window before and after the same edit. A changes from GCT to GTT (A→V); B changes from CTA to TTA (L→L). Use internal codon meanings for these windows, without adding an initiator M.

Result. Window A: A→V, changed = true. Window B: L→L, changed = false.

Final answer:

[
  {
    "frame": "A",
    "original_peptide": "A",
    "edited_peptide": "V",
    "changed": true
  },
  {
    "frame": "B",
    "original_peptide": "L",
    "edited_peptide": "L",
    "changed": false
  }
]

Checking the answer. All four peptide strings and the changed/unchanged flags must agree with the annotated windows and replacement.

Change one frame, preserve the otheroverlap.constrained_editChange DNA so one annotated coding window encodes a requested peptide while the overlapping window’s peptide stays unchanged.

Change one frame, preserve the other

The two coding windows and their strands are supplied, together with an exact target peptide for the first and a list of DNA positions allowed to change. The original second-window peptide is the product that must be preserved.

Search substitutions at those shared DNA positions and evaluate both translations after every candidate choice. A synonymous change in one window may alter the other, so separately choosing codons for the two peptides is insufficient. Use the same internal-translation convention as the overlap-comparison task.

Practical context

The overlap-comparison task describes a real shared-exon example. When one DNA segment encodes two products, a mutation intended for one can recode the other. This task searches exact peptide-preserving constraints, and the verification composition reports both products so the intended protection can be checked.

Method reference: NCBI CDKN2A annotation.

Example

Inputs. DNA ATG GCT AAA TAA; plus-strand windows A = [4,6], B = [5,7]; target A peptide V; only base 5 may change.

Procedure. Try A, C, G, and T at the permitted position and translate both windows for each candidate. T makes window A GTT (V) while changing B from CTA to synonymous TTA (L). Reject candidates unless both peptide conditions hold.

Result. ATG GTT AAA TAA: target A is V, protected B remains L.

Final answer:

ATGGTTAAATAA

Checking the answer. One final DNA sequence must satisfy both peptide requirements and the edit permissions. Return IMPOSSIBLE when the coupled constraints have no solution.

Composition tasks (19)

Each composition task lists the tasks it combines and explains how one task’s output is used by another. Some run tasks in sequence, some use the same result for several calculations, and others require one sequence to satisfy several conditions at once.

Composition types

Pipeline: CDS → protein → peptide intervals → DNA intervals.
Branch: one protein → mass, charge, and composition.
Joint: one CDS must preserve protein, remove sites, and meet GC bounds simultaneously.

For a joint design, completing one rewrite and then another can undo earlier constraints. Every condition must be checked on the same final sequence.

Select Details to read the sequence of operations, an example, and the final success conditions. The component-task links open the corresponding task explanations. Each composition also includes paired prompt templates.
Composition tasks
TaskDescriptionExpand details
From peptide motif to encoding DNApipeline.motif_to_dnaFind a supplied pattern in the CDS’s encoded protein, then report the DNA intervals encoding those protein matches.

From peptide motif to encoding DNA

The input is a CDS plus an amino-acid pattern. First translate the CDS and find all matching residue intervals. For each match, map that interval back to the original DNA using the known reading frame. This asks the model to search at one biological level and report locations at another, rather than searching for the protein letters in DNA.

Practical context

This prepares a protein-level feature for DNA engineering: locate the supplied motif and identify the codons that encode it. Those coordinates can feed permitted motif removal or a planned substitution, without asking the model to infer which sequence features are functional.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GCT GGT TAA; peptide pattern AG.

Procedure. Translate to MAG and find AG at residues 2–3. Convert each endpoint to DNA coordinates: first base 3×2−2 = 4, last base 3×3 = 9. Read that interval from the original CDS.

Result. Peptide interval [2,3] maps to DNA [4,9], sequence GCT GGT. Search in protein space, then map the hit back to DNA.

Final answer:

[
  {
    "aa_interval": [
      2,
      3
    ],
    "nt_interval": [
      4,
      9
    ]
  }
]

Checking the answer. Every protein match and its corresponding DNA interval must be correct; overlapping matches remain separate results.

From CDS to defined protein measurementspipeline.protein_propertiesTranslate one CDS and calculate a fixed set of measurements from that same encoded protein.

From CDS to defined protein measurements

The question supplies a CDS, a pH, and pKa values. Translate once, then use the same product for residue counts, mass, mean hydropathy, charge at the supplied pH, and pI. This is a branching composition: no measurement changes the sequence passed to another measurement.

Practical context

This resembles a construct-characterization report: theoretical mass supports product identification, and charge or pI supports purification planning. Hydropathy and composition add descriptive context. The measurements answer separate questions; combining them does not create a general predictor of protein expression or function.

Method references: ExPASy ProtParam documentation, Cytiva ion-exchanger selection guide.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GCT TAA; pH 6; terminal pKa values 8 and 4; standard residue masses and Kyte–Doolittle scores.

Procedure. Translate once to MA, then pass that same protein to each calculation. Count its residues; sum residue masses plus one water; average the two hydropathy scores; sum terminal charges; find the pH where that charge is zero.

Result. Counts {M:1,A:1}; mass ≈220.088 Da; mean hydropathy 1.85; charge at pH 6 0; pI 6.00 for these parameters.

Final answer:

{
  "residue_counts": {
    "A": 1,
    "M": 1
  },
  "mass_da": 220.0882,
  "mean_hydropathy": 1.8500,
  "charge": 0.0000,
  "pi": 6.00
}

Checking the answer. Each named measurement is checked under its own stated convention and numerical precision.

Use monoisotopic neutral mass of an unmodified linear peptide with free termini. Sum incorporated residue masses and add one H2O (18.010565 Da), once per peptide. Exclude the stop symbol. Residue masses (Da): A=71.037114 C=103.009185 D=115.026943 E=129.042593 F=147.068414 G=57.021464 H=137.058912 I=113.084064 K=128.094963 L=113.084064 M=131.040485 N=114.042927 P=97.052764 Q=128.058578 R=156.101111 S=87.032028 T=101.047679 V=99.068414 W=186.079313 Y=163.063329.

Kyte–Doolittle residue scores: A=1.8 R=-4.5 N=-3.5 D=-3.5 C=2.5 Q=-3.5 E=-3.5 G=-0.4 H=-3.2 I=4.5 L=3.8 K=-3.9 M=1.9 F=2.8 P=-1.6 S=-0.8 T=-0.7 W=-0.9 Y=-1.3 V=4.2. Mean hydropathy is the arithmetic mean of residue scores; it is not a membrane-protein classifier.

Independent-site Henderson–Hasselbalch model: a basic site contributes +1/(1+10^(pH−pKa)); an acidic site contributes −1/(1+10^(pKa−pH)). Count one N terminus (basic), one C terminus (acidic), each K/R/H side chain (basic), and each D/E/C/Y side chain (acidic). All other residues contribute zero. Sum every site. No disulfides, modifications, or environment-dependent shifts. The instance supplies pKa values in both variants.

From CDS panel to a diagnostic peptidepipeline.diagnostic_digestFrom target and comparison CDSs, identify a protein-digest peptide that distinguishes the target from the supplied panel.

From CDS panel to a diagnostic peptide

Start with one target CDS encoding the protein you want to identify, and comparison CDSs encoding the other proteins you want to distinguish it from. The comparison set is called the background in the input fields. Translate every CDS and digest every protein using the same trypsin rule. Discard target peptides also found in any comparison digest, then apply the peptide-length limits. Choose the shortest remaining peptide, breaking ties alphabetically; return NONE if none remains. The result distinguishes the target only from the supplied comparison set.

Practical context

This is a first stage in choosing a proteomics readout that distinguishes related proteins. Deriving the peptide from each actual CDS checks that its uniqueness survives translation and digestion. Experimental assay development must then establish that the candidate peptide is observable and measurable.

Method reference: ExPASy PeptideMass documentation.

Example

Inputs. Target CDS ATG GCT AAA GCT GGT AAA TAA; one comparison CDS ATG GCT AAA GGT GCT AAA TAA. Peptides must be exactly 3 amino acids long.

Procedure. The CDSs differ at codons 4–5: the target has GCT GGT (Ala–Gly), while the comparison has GGT GCT (Gly–Ala). Translate to target MAKAGK and comparison MAKGAK. Trypsin digestion gives target MAK | AGK and comparison MAK | GAK. Discard MAK because both proteins produce it. The remaining target peptide, AGK, meets the length requirement.

Result. AGK. It distinguishes the target from this comparison protein because only the target digest contains it. If the comparison CDS were identical to the target, no peptide would qualify and the answer would be NONE.

Final answer:

AGK

Checking the answer. The final peptide must be eligible and correctly selected from the actual translated-and-digested products, or NONE must be justified by the absence of eligible peptides.

Component tasks

Translate DNA to proteincds.translate→Digest with trypsin rulesprotein.trypsin_digest→Select a distinguishing peptideprotein.diagnostic_peptide

output_format = scalar

  • Return the complete uppercase one-letter amino-acid string without spaces, quotes, a FASTA header, or a terminal stop symbol.
  • Return NONE if no target-only peptide meets the length limits.

Selection. From eligible target-only peptide sequences, choose the shortest, then the ASCII-lexicographically smallest sequence. Multiple copies of one sequence do not create separate choices.

When there is no result or no feasible design:

NONE
Steps and final output+

Translate and digest the target CDS and each comparison CDS (the background set). Compare the target peptides with all comparison peptides. Select the shortest target-only peptide, breaking ties alphabetically, or return NONE if no peptide meets the length limits.

Output: one peptide or NONE

From DNA edits to changed peptide readoutspipeline.variant_peptidesApply DNA edits and determine which tryptic peptide sequences are lost or gained relative to the original CDS.

From DNA edits to changed peptide readouts

Keep two branches: the original CDS and a copy with the supplied DNA edits. Translate and digest both. Compare their peptide-sequence sets to identify readouts removed or introduced by the edit. An edit can change not only a peptide’s letters but also a cleavage site and therefore the fragment boundaries.

Practical context

An engineered DNA change can alter a peptide sequence or create or remove a cleavage boundary. Following both branches identifies candidate readouts for checking whether the edited protein product was made, before developing a mass-spectrometry assay around those products.

Method reference: ExPASy PeptideMass documentation.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GCT AAA GCT GGT AAA TAA; replace bases 7–9, AAA, with GCT.

Procedure. Keep the original and edited branches. Translation changes MAKAGK to MAAAGK. Digest both: original fragments are MAK and AGK; removing the internal K merges them into MAAAGK. Compare the fragment-sequence sets.

Result. Lost {MAK,AGK}; gained {MAAAGK}. Recompute cleavage boundaries after the edit rather than editing an old peptide list.

Final answer:

{
  "lost": [
    "AGK",
    "MAK"
  ],
  "gained": [
    "MAAAGK"
  ]
}

Checking the answer. Both lost and gained sets must match the two digests. This composition ignores peptide multiplicity when taking those set differences.

From specified RNA edits to proteinpipeline.rna_edit_translationTranscribe a CDS, apply supplied RNA edits, and translate the edited RNA to obtain the final protein.

From specified RNA edits to protein

The CDS gives the initial coding RNA, and the question states the exact RNA edits. Apply those edits before translating. The original DNA is retained as the source, but it must not be used in place of the edited RNA at the final step. This tests the consequence of a change introduced specifically at the RNA stage.

Practical context

ApoB provides a direct biological counterpart: APOBEC1-mediated C-to-U editing turns a CAA glutamine codon into a UAA stop, producing a shorter protein. The worked example uses that same codon change on a small illustrative CDS. The edit is supplied; predicting the enzyme’s site selection is outside the task.

Method references: ApoB RNA editing: CAA becomes a stop codon, The apoB-editing catalytic subunit is a cytidine deaminase.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG CAA GGT TAA; supplied RNA edit sets position 4 from C to U.

Procedure. Transcribe to AUG CAA GGU UAA, then edit to AUG UAA GGU UAA. Translate this edited RNA from the original start. Its second codon is now a stop, so do not translate the later GGU.

Result. Final protein M; the original unedited CDS would have given MQG.

Final answer:

M

Checking the answer. The final amino-acid sequence must be the translation of the edited RNA under the specified start and stop conventions.

From specified RNA edits to RNA fragmentspipeline.rna_edit_digestApply specified edits to a CDS-derived RNA and determine the RNA fragments produced afterward by RNase T1.

From specified RNA edits to RNA fragments

Transcribe the CDS, apply the supplied RNA edits, then use the sequence-only RNase T1 rule on that edited RNA. Editing can change a fragment’s letters even when the cuts stay fixed; literal substitutions that add or remove G can also change cut positions. This composition uses explicit A/C/G/U letters. Treating inosine as G for translation does not establish RNase T1 cleavage chemistry at inosine.

Practical context

A supplied RNA edit changes the sequence fingerprint expected from a real RNase T1 digest. The example uses C→U, as in apoB editing: it changes letters within a fragment without changing the G-dependent cuts. This is sequence interpretation for RNA characterization, with mass spectrometry providing a possible downstream readout.

Method references: RNase T1: enzyme specificity and applications, RNA and mRNA sequence mapping by mass spectrometry.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG CAA GGT TAA; RNA position 4 changes C→U; sequence-only RNase T1 mode.

Procedure. Transcribe and edit to AUG UAA GGU UAA. G remains at positions 3, 7, and 8, so cut after those bases. The original second fragment was CAAG; after editing it is UAAG. The cut coordinates are unchanged, but the fragment sequence records the edit.

Result. [(1,3,AUG), (4,7,UAAG), (8,8,G), (9,12,UUAA)].

From a pairing annotation to eligible cutspipeline.structure_gated_digestUse a supplied RNA-structure annotation to decide which RNase T1 cuts are allowed in coding RNA.

From a pairing annotation to eligible cuts

The question supplies a CDS and a dot-bracket annotation of its coding RNA. Convert the annotation into paired positions, then permit cleavage only at G bases marked unpaired. The structure stays fixed for the calculation; the model is not asked to refold fragments after cutting.

Exercise scope

RNase T1 preferentially cleaves single-stranded G sites; RNA protection assays exploit the difference between exposed and protected RNA. That gives the composition a biochemical basis. Its fixed pairing map and binary cut/no-cut mask simplify actual accessibility and reaction kinetics rather than predicting an experimental digestion pattern.

Method reference: RNase T1: enzyme specificity and applications.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GCT TAA; RNA annotation (.(.).)..; RNase T1 accessibility = unpaired only.

Procedure. Transcribe to AUGGCUUAA and decode pairs (1,7),(3,5). The G at 3 is paired, so its cut is blocked; G at 4 is unpaired, so cut after 4. Keep the supplied map fixed throughout.

Result. [(1,4,AUGG), (5,9,CUUAA)]. The annotation changes which sequence-eligible G bases can be cut.

    "end": 4,
    "fragment": "AUGG"

Remove cloning sites while controlling GC

The input supplies forbidden patterns, a strand-search rule, and local GC limits. Both requirements apply to the same final CDS. Removing a site and then fixing GC can recreate the site, so a sequence is accepted only after all checks pass together. The encoded protein and fixed terminal codons must also be preserved.

Practical context

This combines two ordinary construct-design requirements: remove internal sites that would interfere with an assembly method and avoid unsuitable local GC while keeping the protein fixed. Practical constraint-based tools handle this kind of simultaneous repair, because fixing one feature can create another violation.

Method references: GoldenMutagenesis domestication, DNA Chisel examples.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GAA TTC TGA; forbid forward GAATTC; six-base GC windows must contain 2–3 G/C bases.

Procedure. Try synonymous encodings and test both constraints on each whole candidate. GAA→GAG removes GAATTC. Its seven six-base windows contain 3,3,3,3,2,3,2 G/C bases, all permitted. Translate to verify protein preservation.

Result. ATG GAG TTC TGA, encoding MEF, is motif-free and satisfies every GC window simultaneously.

Final answer:

ATGGAGTTCTGA

A synonymous codon change substitutes a codon with another codon encoding the same amino acid. A synonymous CDS rewrite preserves the complete translated protein, length, first codon, and terminal stop codon; no insertions/deletions or new stops. Keep the first and last codons unchanged. Codon boundaries begin at nucleotide 1. Constraints must also be checked across neighboring codon boundaries.

IUPAC DNA ambiguity: A=A; C=C; G=G; T=T; R=AG; Y=CT; S=CG; W=AT; K=GT; M=AC; B=CGT; D=AGT; H=ACT; V=ACG; N=ACGT. An ambiguous symbol represents a set, not a fifth nucleotide. Different positions expand independently.

A coding DNA strand is written 5′→3′. Its coding RNA has the same order of bases with U in place of T. The opposite strand is antiparallel. DNA complement: A↔T, C↔G. A reverse complement complements every base and reverses the sequence.

GC fraction = (number of G + number of C) / number of nucleotides. A window of width w includes every consecutive w-base substring at stride 1. GC3 uses the third nucleotide of each sense codon; exclude the terminal stop codon.

Repair RNA pairs and verify the proteinpipeline.repair_and_verifyRepair specified coding-RNA pairs through synonymous DNA edits, then verify both pairing and protein preservation.

Repair RNA pairs and verify the protein

The question gives the original CDS, intended RNA pairs, and positions allowed to change. Propose a synonymous repair, transcribe that candidate, and check its pairs. Independently compare the candidate’s protein with the original protein. This makes both conditions explicit rather than treating one as a consequence of the other.

Practical context

The rpsT compensatory-mutation study supplies a concrete precedent for repairing proposed coding-RNA contacts through synonymous changes. This composition verifies that the designed sequence restores the specified pairs and retains the protein. A resulting sequence is a candidate experimental control; the pair check alone cannot establish its fitness effect.

Method reference: Synonymous mutations and restoration of mRNA base pairing.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GGG TAA; required RNA pair (3,6); only DNA base 6 is editable.

Procedure. Propose synonymous GGG→GGC. From that candidate, transcribe and check G–C at positions 3 and 6, replacing the original G–G mismatch. Independently translate both CDSs to MG and verify that the only DNA change is at permitted position 6.

Result. ATG GGC TAA; incompatible-pair list []; protein-equivalent true.

Final answer:

ATGGGCTAA

Checking the answer. One final CDS must pass the RNA-pair check, protein-equivalence check, and edit permissions.

Balance an RNA structural constraint and codon preferencejoint.structure_and_codonsWithin a changed-base budget, preserve the protein and meet an RNA pair-score threshold while maximizing codon preference.

Balance an RNA structural constraint and codon preference

The input gives allowed DNA-change counts, a fixed RNA pair map, pair scores, a minimum total pair score, and codon-preference weights. First define feasible synonymous candidates: each must satisfy the edit range and structural threshold. Among those candidates, maximize codon adaptation index. The structure score is a pass/fail constraint here, not a second objective to maximize.

Exercise scope

The composition models the structure of a multi-objective design problem, but its supplied pair-score threshold is artificial. LinearDesign is a practical counterpart that combines codon adaptation with a thermodynamic RNA-folding objective. The benchmark tests constraint coordination without claiming to reproduce that stability model.

Method reference: LinearDesign.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GGA GGT TAA; change exactly two bases; pair (6,9) must score at least 2. AU/UA score 2, CG/GC score 3. Glycine weights: GGA=1.0, GGT=0.9, GGC=0.4, GGG=0.3.

Procedure. Enumerate synonymous candidates, reject wrong edit counts or invalid pairs, then rank survivors by CAI. GGT GGA gives U–A and CAI √(0.9×1.0) ≈ 0.948683. GGC GGG gives C–G and a higher pair score, but lower CAI √(0.4×0.3) ≈ 0.346410. Compare exact weight products before taking roots or rounding; if products tie, use full DNA order.

Result. ATG GGT GGA TAA is optimal. Once the pair-score threshold is met, maximize CAI, not the pair score.

Final answer:

ATGGGTGGATAA

Checking the answer. The accepted candidate must satisfy every feasibility condition and attain the best codon score among feasible candidates.

Choose an RNA probe and a matched escape controlpipeline.target_and_escapeChoose a target-specific RNA probe, then make a synonymous version of the target that no longer closely matches that same probe.

Choose an RNA probe and a matched escape control

Use the target and comparison CDSs to select the required probe by the probe-selection task’s rules. Keep that selected probe fixed while redesigning the target CDS as an escape control. The redesigned target must preserve its protein and meet the supplied mismatch minimum at every RNA window. The comparisons stay unchanged.

Practical context

This provides a sequence-level analogue of an RNAi target and rescue control: the original RNA matches the reagent, while a synonymous construct preserves the protein and disrupts that match. Actual knockdown and rescue depend on reagent activity; a mismatch threshold is only the design screen.

Method reference: RNAi-resistant rescue in a B-cyclin study.

Example

Inputs. Target CDS ATG GCT TAA; background ATG GGT TAA; probe length 3; background mismatch floor 1; escape mismatch floor 1; only target DNA base 6 may change.

Procedure. Probe selection yields AAG, targeting CUU at RNA positions 5–7; keep this probe fixed. Try synonymous choices at target DNA base 6 and check every RNA window against CUU. GCA, GCC, and GCG all escape exact matching; choose the first DNA string, using GCA.

Result. Probe AAG; escape CDS ATG GCA TAA, still encoding MA. The selected probe and the selected escape sequence are both deterministic.

Final answer:

{
  "status": "ok",
  "probe": "AAG",
  "escape_cds": "ATGGCATAA"
}

Checking the answer. Check probe selection and escape design separately, then verify that the reported probe is the one used to construct the control.

Encode a protein change and remove cloning sitesjoint.protein_edit_and_cloningIntroduce one requested amino-acid change and remove forbidden DNA sites with the fewest total base substitutions.

Encode a protein change and remove cloning sites

The requested mutation defines the target protein: one residue changes and all others remain original. Synonymous edits elsewhere are allowed to remove unwanted DNA sites. Search those choices together and minimize the total number of changed DNA bases, while preserving the fixed first and terminal stop codons. This differs from freezing the locally cheapest codon change before attempting cleanup.

Practical context

This turns a requested amino-acid change into a construct compatible with a chosen assembly method. The final translation checks the desired mutation, while motif checks ensure that unwanted restriction sites were not retained or created by the edits.

Method references: GoldenMutagenesis domestication, Site-directed mutagenesis protocol.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GAT TTC TAA; change residue 2 from D to E; forbid forward GAATTC; minimize total changed DNA bases.

Procedure. Try E codons GAA and GAG and any synonymous F cleanup. GAA TTC costs one change but creates the forbidden site; repairing it to GAA TTT costs two. GAG TTC costs one change and is already motif-free. Compare total changes only among valid final candidates.

Result. ATG GAG TTC TAA, encoding MEF, is optimal with one changed base. The locally first E codon, GAA, is not the best complete construct.

Final answer:

ATGGAGTTCTAA

Checking the answer. The final CDS must encode exactly the requested mutant protein, contain no forbidden sites, and minimize total changes with the stated tie-break.

A synonymous codon change substitutes a codon with another codon encoding the same amino acid. A synonymous CDS rewrite preserves the complete translated protein, length, first codon, and terminal stop codon; no insertions/deletions or new stops. Keep the first and last codons unchanged. Codon boundaries begin at nucleotide 1. Constraints must also be checked across neighboring codon boundaries.

IUPAC DNA ambiguity: A=A; C=C; G=G; T=T; R=AG; Y=CT; S=CG; W=AT; K=GT; M=AC; B=CGT; D=AGT; H=ACT; V=ACG; N=ACGT. An ambiguous symbol represents a set, not a fifth nucleotide. Different positions expand independently.

A coding DNA strand is written 5′→3′. Its coding RNA has the same order of bases with U in place of T. The opposite strand is antiparallel. DNA complement: A↔T, C↔G. A reverse complement complements every base and reverses the sequence.

TASK

Build a tagged construct, cleave it, measure productspipeline.tag_cleave_massAssemble a tagged CDS, translate it, simulate TEV cleavage, and calculate the mass of each resulting fragment.

Build a tagged construct, cleave it, measure products

The input supplies tag and linker DNA plus its placement. Assemble the construct by the stated convention, translate the assembled DNA, and cut the product at the benchmark TEV sites. Then calculate each fragment’s mass separately. This tracks both module assembly and the residues left on each side of cleavage.

Practical context

This follows an affinity-tagged construct through tag removal to expected product identity. Keeping track of the exact cleavage scar matters because the purified target’s sequence and theoretical mass can differ from both the original untagged protein and the full fusion.

Method references: Removal of affinity tags with TEV protease, ExPASy PeptideMass documentation.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GCT TAA; N-terminal tag DNA CAT CAT CAT CAT CAT CAT GAA AAT CTG TAT TTT CAG (His6 followed by ENLYFQ); linker GGT (G).

Procedure. Assemble M + HHHHHH + ENLYFQ + G + A. His6 is the affinity handle; ENLYFQG provides the removable TEV junction. Translate to MHHHHHHENLYFQGA and cut after Q, then calculate each fragment’s mass with its own terminal water.

Result. Fragments [MHHHHHHENLYFQ, GA], with monoisotopic masses approximately [1765.764,146.069] Da. The downstream product keeps the G cleavage scar.

Final answer:

{
  "cds": "ATGCATCATCATCATCATCATGAAAATCTGTATTTTCAGGGTGCTTAA",
  "fragments": [
    {
      "peptide": "MHHHHHHENLYFQ",
      "mass_da": 1765.7644
    },
    {
      "peptide": "GA",
      "mass_da": 146.0691
    }
  ]
}

Checking the answer. Check the constructed DNA, all cleavage-product sequences, and each fragment’s calculated mass.

Benchmark TEV cleavage rule: recognize ENLYFQG and cleave ENLYFQ|G. The G remains on the downstream product. Match the complete seven-residue sequence; cut all matches. This is the benchmark exact-match model.

Use monoisotopic neutral mass of an unmodified linear peptide with free termini. Sum incorporated residue masses and add one H2O (18.010565 Da), once per peptide. Exclude the stop symbol. Residue masses (Da): A=71.037114 C=103.009185 D=115.026943 E=129.042593 F=147.068414 G=57.021464 H=137.058912 I=113.084064 K=128.094963 L=113.084064 M=131.040485 N=114.042927 P=97.052764 Q=128.058578 R=156.101111 S=87.032028 T=101.047679 V=99.068414 W=186.079313 Y=163.063329.

Design a codon library and verify its coveragepipeline.library_and_verifyDesign a degenerate codon for requested amino acids, then expand it to verify coverage and absence of stops.

Design a codon library and verify its coverage

Choose the IUPAC codon under the focused-library task’s optimization rules. Insert that notation at the selected internal CDS position, enumerate every concrete codon, and count its protein products. The final enumeration checks what the compact notation actually permits rather than relying on the intended target list.

Practical context

This connects the intent of a focused mutagenesis library to what will actually be synthesized. Enumerating the proposed degenerate codon checks target amino-acid coverage, unintended products, and stops before ordering the oligonucleotide mixture.

Method reference: SwiftLib.

Example

Inputs. CDS ATG GAT TAA; internal codon 2 must cover {D,E} under the focused-library ranking.

Procedure. Select GAK, then insert it as ATG GAK TAA. Independently expand K=G/T: GAG gives E and GAT gives D. Count the resulting products and check whether any expansion is a stop.

Result. Codon GAK; residue counts D=1 and E=1. Both concrete codons are stop-free, and the counts concern this one codon rather than the complete protein.

Final answer:

{
  "status": "ok",
  "codon": "GAK",
  "residue_counts": {
    "D": 1,
    "E": 1
  }
}

Checking the answer. The chosen codon must be optimal under the declared objective, and its reported residue multiplicities must match its full expansion.

Assemble coding modules and locate junction motifspipeline.fusion_junctionJoin two CDS modules, find peptide-pattern matches in the fusion product, and map those matches to the fused DNA.

Assemble coding modules and locate junction motifs

Assemble the modules using the supplied linker and start/stop convention, then translate the fusion. Search the whole protein, including patterns formed across a module junction. Map each result to coordinates in the new fused CDS, not to the coordinate systems of the two original inputs.

Practical context

A fusion can introduce a peptide feature that neither module contains on its own. Checking across each junction and mapping a hit back to DNA supplies the information needed for a subsequent allowed repair, such as removing an unwanted protease site.

Example

Inputs. CDS A ATG GCT TAA; CDS B ATG GGT TGA; empty linker; search peptide AG.

Procedure. Remove A’s stop and B’s initiator, join to ATG GCT GGT TGA, and translate to MAG. AG spans the junction at residues 2–3 even though neither original protein contains AG. Map the hit using the fused sequence’s coordinates.

Result. Fused CDS ATG GCT GGT TGA; motif [2,3]; fused-DNA interval [4,9].

Final answer:

  "fused_cds": "ATGGCTGGTTGA",
  "matches": [

      "aa_interval": [
        2,
        3
      ],
      "nt_interval": [
        4,
        9
      ]
    }
  ]
}

Design and verify an RNA-editing-dependent productpipeline.edit_dependent_productDesign a CDS that preserves the original protein before RNA editing and gives a specified protein after the supplied edits.

Design and verify an RNA-editing-dependent product

First find a permitted synonymous encoding satisfying the editing-dependent design task. Then verify two branches from that same candidate: ordinary translation must produce the original protein, and transcription followed by the supplied RNA edits and translation must produce the target protein. Returning both proteins makes the two requirements inspectable.

Exercise scope

ADAR-mediated RNA recoding is the biological inspiration for the revised A→G translation example. The two branches check the unedited protein and the product implied by the supplied edit. This audits encoding logic; it does not design an ADAR recognition site, guide, or editing reaction.

Method reference: Programmable editing by endogenous ADAR.

Example

Inputs. Reference CDS ATG TCT TAA; only DNA bases 4 and 5 are editable; supplied RNA recoding sets position 4 to G; desired edited protein MG. A→G represents the decoding of A-to-I editing in this translation-only example.

Procedure. Choose synonymous AGT at codon 2. Verify the same candidate in two branches: ATG AGT TAA directly translates to MS, matching the reference. Its RNA AUG AGU UAA becomes AUG GGU UAA after the supplied recoding, translating to MG.

Result. Candidate ATG AGT TAA; unedited product MS; edited product MG. Whether the editing enzyme acts is not evaluated.

Final answer:

{
  "status": "ok",
  "cds": "ATGAGTTAA",
  "unedited_protein": "MS",
  "edited_protein": "MG"
}

Checking the answer. Verify the DNA permissions and both exact protein products on the same designed sequence.

A synonymous codon change substitutes a codon with another codon encoding the same amino acid. A synonymous CDS rewrite preserves the complete translated protein, length, first codon, and terminal stop codon; no insertions/deletions or new stops. Keep the first and last codons unchanged. Codon boundaries begin at nucleotide 1. Constraints must also be checked across neighboring codon boundaries.

A coding DNA strand is written 5′→3′. Its coding RNA has the same order of bases with U in place of T. The opposite strand is antiparallel. DNA complement: A↔T, C↔G. A reverse complement complements every base and reverses the sequence.

Edits use original, 1-based coordinates. A replacement [a,b,text] replaces inclusive interval a..b with text, which may be empty. An insertion at boundary k inserts after original base k (0 means before base 1). Listed edits never overlap and apply simultaneously; later edits are not renumbered. RNA substitutions are specified on the coding RNA after T→U.

TASK

Rules: Only editable_positions may change; first/last codons fixed. Candidate unedited protein equals original. Transcribe candidate, apply exactly the supplied original-coordinate RNA substitutions, then translate to target_protein. Return both proteins.
Steps: Translate the candidate CDS unchanged and verify that it encodes the original protein. Separately, transcribe the same candidate, apply the exact supplied RNA edits, and translate the edited RNA to verify target_protein. Apply the RNA edits to RNA, using its U alphabet.

Edit one frame and audit both productspipeline.overlap_edit_verifyDesign a change for one annotated coding window while preserving the overlapping product, then report both before-and-after peptides.

Edit one frame and audit both products

Use the supplied windows, strands, target peptide, and edit permissions to design DNA. Compare original and designed DNA by translating each window under the overlap task’s internal-codon convention. The explicit before/after output checks both the intended change and the product that must stay fixed.

Practical context

This is a construct audit for a known coding overlap. Reporting both original and edited products verifies that the desired peptide change was achieved without silently altering the protected product. Its scope is sequence preservation under supplied annotations, rather than functional design of new overlapping genes.

Example

Inputs. DNA ATG GCT AAA TAA; plus-strand windows A [4,6] and B [5,7]; target A=V; only base 5 is editable.

Procedure. Design C→T at base 5. Re-extract both windows from the original and candidate DNA: A is GCT→GTT (A→V), B is CTA→TTA (L→L). Compare the entire protected peptide, even when one changed base belongs to both windows.

Result. Candidate ATG GTT AAA TAA; A A→V; B L→L. The requested change and protection checks both pass.

A coding DNA strand is written 5′→3′. Its coding RNA has the same order of bases with U in place of T. The opposite strand is antiparallel. DNA complement: A↔T, C↔G. A reverse complement complements every base and reverses the sequence.

Edits use original, 1-based coordinates. A replacement [a,b,text] replaces inclusive interval a..b with text, which may be empty. An insertion at boundary k inserts after original base k (0 means before base 1). Listed edits never overlap and apply simultaneously; later edits are not renumbered. RNA substitutions are specified on the coding RNA after T→U.

Build and audit a controlled synonymous panelpipeline.controlled_panelGenerate matched synonymous CDSs with different CG targets, then report their measured RNA CG counts and DNA GC fractions.

Build and audit a controlled synonymous panel

Design a panel in which each member meets its assigned coding-RNA CG count and all share the requested total number of G/C bases. Transcribe and measure each actual candidate, and compare its translated protein with the original. This connects design targets to independently checkable measurements.

Practical context

This prepares and audits sequences for a controlled synonymous comparison: protein identity and total GC stay fixed while CG count varies. Such panels can support experiments measuring RNA abundance or protein output. Independent measurements of each designed sequence distinguish achieved controls from merely requested ones.

Method reference: Coding-sequence determinants of expression.

Example

Inputs. Reference ATG GCT GGC TAA; desired CG counts [0,1]; shared G/C count 6.

Procedure. Choose the canonical complete panel in the requested CG-count order: ATG GCA GGC TAA and ATG GCC GGA TAA. For each actual sequence, transcribe and count adjacent CGs, count all DNA G/C bases, and translate. Both have six G/C bases among twelve DNA bases; their RNA CG counts are 0 and 1.

Result. The ordered records report those two CDSs with CG counts 0 and 1 and GC fractions 0.500000 each. Both proteins are MAG; the final JSON records include the selected sequences as well as their measurements.

Final answer:

{
  "status": "ok",
  "members": [
    {
      "cds": "ATGGCAGGCTAA",
      "cg_count": 0,
      "gc_fraction": 0.500000
    },
    {
      "cds": "ATGGCCGGATAA",
      "cg_count": 1,
      "gc_fraction": 0.500000
    }
  ]
}

Checking the answer. Every sequence must satisfy its own CG target, the shared GC requirement, protein identity, and the fixed terminal-codon rule.

  • When no complete panel exists, return status=impossible and members=null.
